# Why Rust: A Technical Rationale for the Alma Backend

> A whitepaper-style justification for implementing the Alma backend in Rust,
> grounded in peer-reviewed literature and industry security data. All bracketed
> citations `[n]` resolve to the **References** at the end of this rationale.

## Abstract

The choice of implementation language is an architectural decision with
consequences that persist for the lifetime of a system: it determines which
classes of defect are possible, how the system behaves under concurrency and
load, and how much of a program's correctness can be established before it ever
runs. This document sets out, in eight parts, the technical case for building the
Alma backend in Rust. It begins with the criteria against which a systems
language should be judged, surveys the memory-safety crisis that has driven
governments and major vendors toward memory-safe languages [10][13][14][15][16],
explains the ownership model and its formal foundations [1][2][3][4][18], and
examines concurrency [19], performance and efficiency [9], and the empirical
record of Rust in production [5][6][7][8]. It closes by grounding these
properties in Alma's own design and by stating the trade-offs honestly. The
conclusion is not that Rust is without cost, but that for a long-lived,
concurrent, security-sensitive HTTP backend it satisfies the relevant criteria
simultaneously in a way no mainstream alternative currently does.

## 1. Language Choice as an Architectural Decision

The selection of an implementation language is frequently treated as a matter of team familiarity or ecosystem convenience, resolved implicitly and rarely revisited. For alma this decision is treated instead as a first-class architectural concern, on the same footing as the choice of a hexagonal, ports-and-adapters structure or the adoption of an asynchronous request model. The reasoning is straightforward: the language determines the class of defects that are possible at all, the guarantees the compiler can enforce before code reaches production, and the performance envelope within which every subsequent design decision must operate. These properties are not easily changed later. Unlike a caching layer or a serialization format, the implementation language is not a component that can be swapped behind a port; it pervades every adapter, every domain module, and every line of the runtime. A language choice therefore constrains the achievable properties of the system for its entire lifetime, and it warrants the same deliberate evaluation applied to any load-bearing architectural element.

alma is a modular HTTP backend built on the axum web framework over the tokio asynchronous runtime, organized according to the hexagonal architecture pattern. The domain core is isolated behind explicit ports; adapters bind those ports to concrete infrastructure such as HTTP transport, persistence, and external services. This structure presupposes two things from the underlying language. First, it presupposes strong support for expressing and enforcing boundaries — the compiler must be able to prevent the domain core from depending on incidental infrastructure detail, and it must make interface contracts explicit and checkable. Second, because the runtime is concurrent and I/O-bound, it presupposes a concurrency model whose safety does not degrade as the number of adapters and in-flight requests grows. The evaluation of candidate languages was conducted against these presuppositions rather than against surface-level ergonomics.

### Evaluation criteria

The candidate languages were assessed against six criteria, each of which maps to a concrete risk or cost borne over the operational life of the service.

| Criterion | Concern it addresses |
|---|---|
| Memory safety | Elimination of use-after-free, buffer overflow, and related defects that dominate security-critical bug classes |
| Data-race freedom | Correctness of the concurrent request-handling core under load |
| Runtime performance and latency predictability | Sustained throughput and bounded tail latency without stop-the-world pauses |
| Compile-time enforcement of invariants | Shifting defect detection left, from production to the build |
| Long-term maintainability | Refactoring safety and the durability of interface contracts |
| Total cost of ownership | Infrastructure, incident, and personnel costs across the service lifetime |

These criteria are not independent. Memory safety and data-race freedom are, in most language families, in direct tension with runtime performance: the conventional means of achieving the former — a tracing garbage collector and a managed runtime — introduces the latency variability and resource overhead that undermine the latter. This tension is the crux of the language decision and is examined in the subsections that follow.

**Memory safety and data-race freedom.** The importance of these two criteria is grounded in empirical evidence about where serious defects originate. Analyses of large codebases by major vendors have repeatedly found that memory-safety violations account for a majority of severe security vulnerabilities: approximately 70% of the CVEs assigned by the Microsoft Security Response Center over a multi-year period were memory-safety issues [10], and the Chromium project reports a comparable figure, with roughly 70% of its serious security bugs attributable to memory-safety errors [16]. A language that structurally excludes these defect classes removes the largest single category of security risk from consideration rather than mitigating it after the fact. For a concurrent backend, data-race freedom is the analogous property in the temporal dimension: races produce intermittent, load-dependent failures that are among the most costly defects to diagnose and reproduce.

**Performance and latency predictability.** As an I/O-bound service handling concurrent requests, alma is sensitive not only to mean throughput but to the predictability of latency at the tail. Managed runtimes introduce garbage-collection pauses whose timing is not under application control, coupling worst-case latency to allocation behavior elsewhere in the process. A model based on deterministic, compile-time-scheduled resource release avoids this class of variability. Performance also has a direct cost dimension: comparative measurements across programming languages indicate substantial differences in execution time and energy consumption, with compiled, non-managed languages occupying the efficient end of the spectrum [9]. Lower per-request resource consumption translates directly into reduced infrastructure cost at a given service level.

**Compile-time enforcement and maintainability.** The value of shifting defect detection to compile time compounds over the maintenance life of a system. Invariants that the compiler enforces cannot regress silently during refactoring, which is precisely the activity a hexagonal architecture is designed to make routine. The stronger the guarantees the type system can carry across module boundaries, the safer large-scale change becomes, and the lower the long-run maintenance burden.

### Thesis

The central claim of this rationale is that Rust satisfies these six criteria simultaneously, and that this simultaneity — rather than excellence on any single axis — is what distinguishes it. Rust was designed to occupy the intersection that the conventional trade-off treats as empty: it provides memory safety and data-race freedom without a garbage collector, enforcing both at compile time through its ownership and borrowing discipline while compiling to native code with performance characteristics comparable to C and C++ [2][4]. The safety guarantees are not conventions or lint rules but properties the type system enforces before a binary is produced, and they extend into the concurrency domain, where the same ownership model that prevents memory errors also statically excludes data races [2]. This combination allows the performance and latency criteria to be met without sacrificing the safety criteria, dissolving the tension that forces most languages to compromise on one or the other.

Two qualifications are stated here and developed in later sections. First, Rust's guarantees hold for code written in its safe subset; the language admits an `unsafe` escape hatch whose use shifts specific obligations back to the programmer, and the discipline surrounding that boundary is itself an engineering concern rather than an automatic guarantee. Second, the strength of the compiler's enforcement carries a corresponding learning and initial-development cost, which must be weighed against the total cost of ownership rather than assessed in isolation. Both qualifications are addressed on their merits in the sections that follow; neither undermines the thesis that, among the languages evaluated, Rust is uniquely positioned to satisfy alma's architectural criteria together rather than in part.
## 2. The Memory-Safety Problem in Systems Software

Systems software—operating system kernels, browsers, network stacks, cryptographic libraries, and runtimes—has historically been written in C and C++. These languages offer the low-level control and predictable performance that systems work demands, but they delegate the management of memory to the programmer and provide no enforced guarantee that memory is accessed correctly. A large body of evidence accumulated by the organizations that maintain the most heavily scrutinized codebases in the world now indicates that this delegation is the dominant source of serious security vulnerabilities.

### 2.1 The empirical weight of memory-safety defects

The most frequently cited figure comes from Microsoft's Security Response Center, which reported that approximately 70% of the CVEs assigned by Microsoft each year address memory-safety issues [10]. The Chromium project, which maintains one of the largest and most exposed C++ codebases in production, reports an almost identical proportion: roughly 70% of its serious security bugs are memory-safety problems [16]. That two independently maintained, architecturally distinct, and security-critical codebases converge on the same proportion is significant. It suggests the figure is not an artifact of a particular product, team, or review process, but a structural property of large systems written in memory-unsafe languages.

The Android platform provides a longitudinal complement to these point estimates. Google reported that memory-safety defects consistently accounted for the majority of Android's high-severity security vulnerabilities, and that the share of such vulnerabilities fell as the proportion of new code written in memory-safe languages increased [11]. In subsequent analysis, Google observed that the density of memory-safety vulnerabilities declines sharply as code ages, so that the most effective intervention is to write *new* code in memory-safe languages rather than to attempt exhaustive remediation of existing code—an approach it described as addressing memory safety "at the source" [12]. This reframes the problem from one of finding and fixing individual defects to one of eliminating an entire vulnerability class by construction.

### 2.2 Why C and C++ admit these defects by construction

The vulnerabilities in question are not the result of unusual carelessness; they arise from the ordinary interaction of manual memory management with unrestricted aliasing. C and C++ permit a program to hold multiple pointers to the same object, to free that object through one pointer while others remain live, and to index into a buffer without a bounds check. The language does not track object lifetimes or ownership, so the compiler cannot reject these patterns, and in the general case they cannot be detected statically. The principal bug classes follow directly from this design:

| Bug class | Mechanism | Typical consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Use-after-free | A pointer is dereferenced after the object it refers to has been deallocated | Arbitrary read/write, control-flow hijack |
| Double free | The same allocation is released twice, corrupting allocator metadata | Heap corruption, exploitable state |
| Buffer overflow / out-of-bounds access | A read or write crosses the bounds of an allocation | Memory disclosure, adjacent-object corruption |
| Uninitialized memory use | Memory is read before a defined value is written | Information leak, nondeterministic behavior |
| Data race | Two threads access shared memory concurrently, at least one writing, without synchronization | Undefined behavior, torn reads/writes, corruption |

Each of these is a form of *undefined behavior*: once triggered, the language specification places no constraint on subsequent execution, and an attacker who can influence the affected memory can frequently escalate the defect into remote code execution or privilege escalation. Empirical study of real-world Rust programs confirms that the safety guarantees relevant here concern exactly this set of concerns—memory errors and thread-safety errors such as data races [5]—and that a language which prevents them removes the substrate on which a large fraction of exploits are built.

### 2.3 The defects Rust eliminates by construction

Rust's central contribution is that it makes the majority of these bug classes unrepresentable in safe code, rather than merely detectable after the fact. Its ownership and borrowing discipline enforces, at compile time, that each value has a single owner responsible for its deallocation and that references are either one unique mutable borrow or any number of shared immutable borrows, but never both simultaneously [2][4]. This aliasing discipline is what statically excludes use-after-free, double free, and the write-through-a-dangling-pointer patterns above, and the same "aliasing XOR mutability" invariant that rules out data races is enforced by the same mechanism [2]. Bounds checking closes the remaining gap for buffer overflows at runtime. The formal foundations of these guarantees have been established through machine-checked proofs of soundness for a realistic subset of the language and its libraries [1], including under a relaxed-memory concurrency model [19], giving the informal claim of "safety by construction" a rigorous basis.

This guarantee is qualified rather than absolute, and the qualification matters. Rust provides an `unsafe` escape hatch for operations the compiler cannot verify, and safety of the whole program depends on the correctness of the code inside those blocks. Studies of how the escape hatch is used in practice find that unsafe code is common but tends to be small and localized, often used to interface with foreign code or to implement data structures the borrow checker cannot express [6], and that memory-safety bugs in Rust, where they occur, are frequently connected to such unsafe code [5]. Ecosystem-scale analysis has found real memory-safety defects concentrated in these regions [21]. The value proposition is therefore not that unsafety is impossible, but that it is confined to auditable, explicitly marked boundaries rather than diffused across the entire program.

### 2.4 The institutional response

The scale and consistency of the evidence has produced an unusually direct response from national security and policy institutions. The U.S. National Security Agency issued guidance recommending that organizations shift from memory-unsafe to memory-safe languages where feasible, identifying the same categories of defect—use-after-free, buffer overflows, and related errors—as the target [13]. A joint publication by CISA, the NSA, the FBI, and international partners argued that software manufacturers should publish "memory safe roadmaps" describing how they will move critical components to memory-safe languages [14]. The White House Office of the National Cyber Director subsequently characterized the adoption of memory-safe languages as a way to eliminate an entire class of vulnerabilities and called on the technical community to reduce the attack surface attributable to memory-unsafety in foundational software [15].

Taken together, these positions represent a shift in framing. The prevailing objective is no longer to detect and patch individual memory-safety defects—an activity that the 70% figures suggest has not materially reduced their prevalence over decades—but to adopt languages in which the most severe classes cannot arise in ordinary code. The engineering question that follows is whether a language can provide these guarantees without sacrificing the performance, control, and predictability that made C and C++ the default for systems work in the first place. The remainder of this document addresses that question with reference to Rust.
## 3. Ownership, Borrowing, and Affine Types

Rust's defining contribution is a static discipline for managing memory and other resources that does not depend on a tracing garbage collector and does not defer safety to programmer convention. The mechanism rests on three interlocking rules — ownership, move semantics, and borrowing — enforced at compile time by the type and lifetime checker [4]. Understood through the lens of substructural type theory, these rules approximate an *affine* type system: a value may be used at most once along any control-flow path, and the compiler tracks the point at which responsibility for a value passes from one binding to another. This framing explains why entire categories of memory-safety defects that dominate real-world vulnerability data — use-after-free, double-free, and data races on shared mutable state — become unrepresentable in the safe fragment of the language rather than merely discouraged.

### 3.1 Ownership and move semantics

Every value in Rust has a unique owning binding. When ownership is transferred — by assignment, by passing an argument, or by returning from a function — the source binding is *moved from* and can no longer be used. This is the affine constraint made operational: the value is consumed by the move, and the type checker rejects any subsequent use of the moved-out binding. Ownership also determines deallocation. When the owner goes out of scope, the value's destructor runs and its resources are released. This is the Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) idiom, applied uniformly to heap memory, file handles, locks, and sockets: resource lifetime is bound to a lexical scope and cleanup is automatic, deterministic, and statically located.

The contrast with the two dominant alternatives is precise:

| Property | Manual (C/C++) | Tracing GC (Java, Go, etc.) | Rust ownership |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deallocation timing | Programmer-directed, error-prone | Non-deterministic, runtime | Deterministic, at scope end |
| Use-after-free / double-free | Possible | Prevented | Prevented at compile time |
| Runtime memory overhead | None | GC metadata, heap headroom | None |
| Pause / latency cost | None | GC pauses possible | None |
| Non-memory resources (locks, files) | Manual | Requires explicit disposal | RAII, uniform |

Manual management offers deterministic timing and no runtime overhead but places the full burden of correctness on the programmer; the industry consequence is well documented, with memory-safety errors accounting for roughly 70% of the CVEs assigned by the Microsoft Security Response Center [10] and a comparable share of serious security bugs in Chromium [16]. Tracing garbage collection removes most of these defects but does so at runtime, introducing collection pauses and memory overhead and, notably, addressing memory management without addressing the safe management of other resources. Rust's model targets the same safety guarantees as garbage collection while retaining the deterministic, zero-overhead deallocation characteristic of manual management.

### 3.2 Borrowing: aliasing xor mutability

Requiring unique ownership for every access would be impractical, so Rust permits *borrowing*: the temporary creation of references that do not transfer ownership. Borrowing is governed by a single invariant, often summarized as *aliasing xor mutability*:

- Any number of shared (immutable) references `&T` may coexist, or
- Exactly one mutable reference `&mut T` may exist,

but never both simultaneously. A shared reference grants read access and can be freely duplicated; a mutable reference grants exclusive read-write access and cannot coexist with any other reference to the same value. This is the mechanism by which Rust prevents whole classes of errors at compile time. If mutation is only ever possible through a reference that is provably unaliased, then no other pointer can observe or invalidate a value mid-mutation. Iterator invalidation, concurrent modification, and data races reduce to violations of the same rule and are rejected by the borrow checker before the program runs. The guarantee is structural rather than probabilistic: it does not depend on test coverage or reviewer vigilance.

Lifetimes are the compile-time bookkeeping that makes borrowing sound. A lifetime is a region of the program for which a reference is valid; the checker verifies that no reference outlives the value it points to, so a borrow can never become dangling. Lifetimes carry no runtime representation — they are erased after checking — which is why the discipline imposes no execution cost.

### 3.3 Formal foundations

The claim that these rules are sound, rather than merely conventional, has been the subject of sustained formal study, and this distinguishes Rust's model from ad hoc static analyses. Two lines of work are directly relevant to the ownership and borrowing core.

Oxide provides a formal operational semantics for a substantial subset of Rust in which ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes are given precise typing rules, making explicit the connection between the borrow checker and a substructural type system [18]. It offers a model in which the informal notion of "aliasing xor mutability" is stated as a checkable property of a small-step semantics.

Stacked Borrows supplies an operational aliasing model for Rust that defines, at the level of individual memory accesses, which uses of references are permitted [3]. It specifies a per-location discipline on the order in which references may be created and used, and it serves both as a specification for correct programs and as a basis for detecting undefined behavior — including in code that uses low-level pointer operations. Stacked Borrows makes the aliasing discipline concrete enough to reason about the boundary between the safe language and unsafe code, where the compiler's guarantees must be upheld by the programmer rather than the checker.

### 3.4 Scope and limitations

The guarantees described here apply to the safe fragment of the language. Rust deliberately provides an `unsafe` escape hatch for operations the checker cannot verify — raw pointer dereferences, foreign-function calls, and certain low-level abstractions — and within such blocks the aliasing and lifetime invariants become the programmer's responsibility. The ownership model does not make `unsafe` code safe; it confines the reasoning burden to explicitly demarcated regions, which is where the formal aliasing models [3][18] become the relevant specification. Furthermore, the borrow checker prevents unsafety by rejecting programs it cannot prove sound, which means it also rejects some sound programs, imposing a learning and expressiveness cost that is examined elsewhere in this document. These are real trade-offs. The central result of this section is narrower and defensible: by encoding an affine-style ownership discipline and an aliasing-xor-mutability rule into the type system, and by grounding that discipline in a formal semantics, Rust renders use-after-free, double-free, and data-race defects unrepresentable in safe code — achieving the safety profile of garbage collection without its runtime cost and the determinism of manual management without its hazards [3][4][18].
## 4. Compile-Time Guarantees and Formal Foundations

Rust's central claim is that a well-typed program in the safe fragment of the
language is free from a specific and well-defined class of defects: out-of-bounds
accesses, use-after-free, double-free, invalid pointer dereferences, and data
races on shared memory. This guarantee is not a heuristic produced by a bug
finder or a probabilistic assurance derived from testing; it is a property
enforced statically by the type system and borrow checker at compile time. The
significance of this class of defects is well documented. Independent analyses
across two of the largest software vendors converge on a similar figure: roughly
70% of the security vulnerabilities assigned CVEs by the Microsoft Security
Response Center are memory-safety issues [10], and approximately 70% of serious
security bugs in the Chromium codebase are likewise memory-safety bugs [16]. A
language that can eliminate the bulk of this category at compile time therefore
addresses a substantial fraction of the practical security burden of systems
software.

### 4.1 What the Guarantee Formally Means

Rust's safety guarantee is best understood through the standard soundness
statement for a type system, often summarized as "well-typed programs do not go
wrong." Concretely, the guarantee is that any program accepted by the compiler,
provided it does not use the `unsafe` escape hatch, will not exhibit undefined
behavior of the memory-safety kind at run time. The mechanism underlying this
property is ownership together with borrowing: each value has a unique owner,
references are either a single mutable (exclusive) borrow or any number of shared
(immutable) borrows, and the lifetime of every borrow is constrained so that it
cannot outlive the value it refers to [4]. This discipline statically rules out
aliasing patterns that would otherwise permit a mutation to invalidate a
reference held elsewhere. Data-race freedom follows from the same aliasing
discipline extended across threads: concurrent mutable access to shared state is
inexpressible in safe code without synchronization primitives that themselves
uphold the invariants.

It is important to state the scope precisely. The guarantee is a statement about
the *safe* fragment. It does not claim the absence of all defects. Logic errors,
resource exhaustion, deadlocks, and panics remain possible, and memory *leaks*
are explicitly not prevented, as they do not constitute memory unsafety. The
value of the guarantee lies in its being total over the class it covers within
safe code, rather than partial across all classes.

### 4.2 Why the Guarantee Is Trustworthy: RustBelt

A type system is only as trustworthy as the proof that it is sound. Rust's
surface rules are intricate, and the language ships a large standard library
whose internals rely on low-level operations that the borrow checker cannot
justify directly. This raises an obvious question: if foundational libraries
must reach beneath the safe rules, does the end-to-end safety claim still hold?
The RustBelt project provides the formal answer. RustBelt gives the first formal
soundness proof for a realistic subset of Rust, establishing that the type
system is sound *even in the presence* of the unsafe code used inside standard
libraries, provided that unsafe code respects certain well-defined interface
contracts [1][2].

The proof is constructed in a semantic style. Rather than reasoning only about
syntactic typing rules, RustBelt assigns each type a semantic meaning as a
predicate over machine states and shows that safe combinators preserve those
predicates. For a library that internally uses unsafe operations, the obligation
is to demonstrate that its implementation satisfies the semantic interpretation
of the type it exposes; once discharged, clients may use the library through its
safe interface with full confidence. The formalization is carried out in the
Iris framework, a higher-order concurrent separation logic mechanized in the Coq
proof assistant [1]. Separation logic is the natural tool here because ownership
and borrowing are fundamentally statements about the disjointness and transfer
of ownership of memory, which separation logic is designed to express. Related
work situates this within a broader formal understanding of the language: an
aliasing model that makes precise which pointer operations unsafe code may
perform [3], a core calculus capturing the essence of ownership and borrowing
[18], and an extension of the soundness argument to a relaxed memory model rather
than an idealized sequentially consistent one [19].

The practical import is that the safety guarantee is not merely asserted by the
language designers but underwritten by machine-checked proof for a substantial,
realistic model of the language and its libraries [1][2].

### 4.3 The `unsafe` Escape Hatch and Its Use in Practice

The soundness argument depends on a clear separation between safe and unsafe
code. The `unsafe` keyword marks regions where the programmer takes on
obligations the compiler cannot verify: dereferencing raw pointers, calling
foreign functions, or asserting invariants the borrow checker cannot see. Unsafe
code is necessary because certain correct and efficient data structures cannot
be expressed within the safe rules, and because interaction with hardware and
foreign code is inherently outside the model. The design intent is that unsafe
blocks be small, auditable, and encapsulated behind safe interfaces that
preserve the language's invariants, precisely the pattern RustBelt formalizes.

Empirical study of how `unsafe` is actually used supports this model, with
qualifications. A large-scale analysis of Rust code found that `unsafe` appears
in a minority of functions and is frequently used to interface with existing
non-Rust code or for performance-sensitive operations, and that programmers
often do attempt to isolate it behind safe abstractions [6]. At the same time,
the same body of work and related studies caution that encapsulation is not
always achieved cleanly and that unsafe blocks are sometimes larger or more
entangled with surrounding code than the ideal would suggest [6]. Separately,
analyses of real-world Rust programs have shown that memory- and thread-safety
bugs that do occur are concentrated around unsafe usage and the interaction
between safe and unsafe code [5]. The reasonable conclusion is that Rust
relocates the trusted computing base rather than eliminating it: the burden of
memory-safety reasoning is reduced to a comparatively small, explicitly marked
surface, but that surface still demands discipline and review.

### 4.4 Verification and Analysis Tooling

Because unsafe code carries obligations the compiler does not check, tooling that
targets it and that extends verification beyond the built-in guarantees is a
meaningful complement to the type system. Two representative efforts illustrate
the range.

| Tool | Purpose | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Prusti | Deductive verification of functional correctness and stronger properties, leveraging Rust's type information for modular specification | [20] |
| Rudra | Static analysis for detecting memory-safety bugs in unsafe code at ecosystem scale | [21] |

Prusti builds on Rust's type system to provide modular specification and
verification, using the guarantees the types already supply to reduce the
annotation and proof burden required to establish properties beyond memory safety
[20]. Rudra approaches the problem from the direction of bug finding, applying
static analysis to detect classes of memory-safety defects in unsafe Rust and
demonstrating its effectiveness by scanning the public package ecosystem [21].
Together these represent the two complementary strategies appropriate to the
architecture described above: raising assurance about what the compiler already
accepts, and scrutinizing the unsafe regions the compiler deliberately does not
police.

### 4.5 Summary

The safety guarantee Rust offers is precise in scope and strong within that
scope. For the safe fragment it is a compile-time, total exclusion of a class of
defects that accounts for roughly 70% of serious security vulnerabilities in
large systems [10][16], and it rests on a machine-checked soundness proof that
accounts for realistic libraries [1][2]. The guarantee is not unconditional: it
depends on the correct use of the `unsafe` escape hatch, which in practice is
common but not always cleanly encapsulated [6], and which remains the locus of
most observed safety defects [5]. Verification and analysis tools such as Prusti
[20] and Rudra [21] address, respectively, the properties beyond memory safety
and the unsafe surface that the type system leaves to programmer discipline.
## 5. Fearless Concurrency and the Asynchronous Backend

### 5.1 The problem: data races in concurrent systems

A web backend is, by construction, a concurrent program. Each inbound HTTP request executes on a task that may run in parallel with hundreds of others, and these tasks frequently contend for the same resources: connection pools, in-memory caches, session state, rate-limit counters, and background job queues. In this setting, the dominant class of correctness failures is the *data race* — two threads accessing the same memory location concurrently, with at least one access being a write, and no synchronization ordering the two. Data races are notorious for their nondeterminism: they surface intermittently under load, resist reproduction in test environments, and frequently manifest as silent memory corruption rather than clean failures. Empirical study of production Rust confirms that concurrency is a genuine source of defects rather than a theoretical concern; a systematic analysis of real-world Rust programs and their bug histories found that thread-safety issues, including deadlocks and races arising from the interaction of shared state and synchronization primitives, constitute a distinct and recurring bug category worthy of dedicated tooling [5]. The relevant design question is therefore not whether concurrency bugs occur, but at which point in the development lifecycle they are caught.

### 5.2 The mechanism: ownership plus `Send` and `Sync`

Rust's approach is to reject data races at compile time by extending the ownership and borrowing discipline — the same discipline that governs single-threaded memory safety — across thread boundaries. Two marker traits encode the thread-related properties of a type. A type is `Send` if a value of that type may be safely transferred to another thread, and `Sync` if a reference to it may be shared across threads (equivalently, `&T` is `Send`). These traits are auto-derived: a composite type is `Send`/`Sync` if and only if all of its constituents are, so the property propagates structurally through the type graph without manual annotation in the common case.

The critical interaction is between these traits and the borrow checker's aliasing rule, which permits either a single mutable reference *or* any number of shared references to a value, but never both simultaneously. Because a `&mut T` is unique, the type that holds it cannot be aliased across threads; because a shared `&T` is read-only, concurrent readers cannot race. Mutable state that genuinely must be shared between threads can only be reached through types whose APIs enforce synchronization — for example `Mutex<T>` or `RwLock<T>`, which are `Sync` precisely because they mediate all access through a lock, or atomic types that provide well-defined concurrent semantics. The consequence is a compile-time guarantee: a program that would exhibit a data race fails to typecheck. This is not a lint or a heuristic but a soundness property. It has been established formally: the RustBelt line of work provides a machine-checked semantic model proving that well-typed Rust programs, including those built from libraries containing internal `unsafe` code, are free of undefined behavior [1][2], and RustBelt Meets Relaxed Memory extends that foundation to a *relaxed* (weak) memory model — the setting in which real multicore hardware and the C/C++ memory model actually operate — showing that the guarantees hold under weak-memory semantics rather than only under the simplifying assumption of sequential consistency [19]. The importance of that extension is that data-race freedom claimed only for a sequentially consistent machine would not transfer to production hardware; the relaxed-memory result closes that gap.

### 5.3 Application to alma's tokio/axum backend

alma's backend is an asynchronous HTTP service built on the `tokio` runtime with the `axum` web framework, and its request-handling model is exactly the one described above: many handlers run concurrently, multiplexed by an asynchronous work-stealing scheduler across a pool of worker threads. In an async runtime the guarantees matter more, not less, than in a classical thread-per-request server, because tasks are moved between threads by the scheduler and futures that are held across `.await` points may resume on a different worker. The `Send` bound that `tokio` places on spawned tasks is what makes this migration safe: state captured by a handler and carried across an await must itself be `Send`, and the compiler enforces this at the point of `spawn`. Shared application state — the connection pool, configuration, cached credentials — is threaded through handlers as `Sync` types (typically an `Arc<T>` over an immutable or internally-synchronized value), which the type system verifies is safe to share by shared reference across all concurrent handlers.

The practical effect on alma's development is a shift in *when* concurrency errors are detected:

| Property | Runtime-checked / convention-based (GC languages) | Rust (`Send`/`Sync` + ownership) |
|---|---|---|
| Data-race detection | Runtime, probabilistic, load-dependent | Compile time, deterministic |
| Enforcement of shared-state discipline | Programmer convention, code review | Type system; non-conforming code does not compile |
| Failure mode when violated | Silent corruption or intermittent fault | Build failure |
| Coverage under weak memory | Depends on library correctness | Formally modeled [19] |

The contrast with garbage-collected languages is instructive. A managed runtime eliminates use-after-free and double-free by reclaiming memory automatically, but garbage collection is orthogonal to data-race freedom: it guarantees that a reference remains valid, not that concurrent access to the referent is synchronized. In such languages, freedom from data races on ordinary shared objects rests on programmer discipline and convention — remembering to hold the right lock, to use a concurrent collection, or to confine mutable state to a single thread — checked, if at all, only by review and by tests that must happen to exercise the racing interleaving. Rust moves this obligation into the type system, where it is checked exhaustively rather than sampled.

### 5.4 Scope and limitations

Two qualifications are necessary to avoid overstatement. First, "fearless concurrency" is a claim about data-race freedom, not about all concurrency hazards. Deadlocks, livelocks, and higher-level logical races between operations remain possible in safe Rust, and the empirical record shows these do occur in practice [5]; the type system prevents the specific undefined behavior of unsynchronized memory access, not every scheduling-dependent defect. Second, the guarantees are contingent on the correctness of any `unsafe` code that manually implements `Send`/`Sync` or builds synchronization primitives. The formal soundness results account for such code by requiring that each `unsafe` block uphold the library's specified invariants [1][2][19], but this shifts the obligation to the small set of foundational libraries rather than discharging it entirely — a reason to concentrate `unsafe` in well-audited dependencies and to keep application-level handler code within the safe subset. Within those bounds, the guarantee is strong and directly relevant to alma: every concurrent request handler is checked, at compile time, against the class of errors most likely to corrupt shared state under production load.
## 6. Performance, Predictability, and Efficiency

A backend that serves production traffic is judged not only by whether it produces correct results, but by how consistently and economically it produces them under load. Three properties matter in combination: raw throughput, the predictability of latency (particularly at the tail of the distribution), and the resource footprint required to sustain a given level of service. Rust's design targets all three simultaneously, and it does so without asking the developer to trade away the memory- and thread-safety guarantees discussed in earlier sections. This section explains the mechanisms that make this possible, situates Rust's efficiency against empirical measurements, and states the limits of what these properties can be expected to deliver.

### 6.1 Zero-cost abstractions

The central performance principle Rust inherits from the C++ tradition is that abstractions should not impose a runtime penalty beyond what an expert would pay by writing the equivalent lower-level code by hand. High-level constructs — iterators, closures, generic functions, trait-based polymorphism, and the ownership types that enforce safety — are resolved and specialized at compile time. Generic code is monomorphized, meaning a distinct, type-specialized version is generated for each concrete instantiation, so that dispatch is static and inlinable rather than deferred to runtime. Iterator chains compile down to loops comparable to hand-written imperative equivalents. The ownership and borrowing discipline that underpins Rust's safety guarantees is likewise a compile-time construct: the borrow checker performs its analysis statically and emits no runtime bookkeeping, so the safety story does not translate into per-operation cost [4]. Formal work on Rust's foundations has established that these guarantees hold soundly even in the presence of the language's carefully scoped `unsafe` escape hatch, which is what allows performance-critical internals to be written without abandoning the overall safety model [1][2]. In other words, the abstractions used to make code safe and readable are the same abstractions the compiler is able to erase.

### 6.2 No garbage collector, and the consequences for tail latency

The most consequential architectural decision for predictability is that Rust manages memory through ownership and deterministic destruction rather than through a garbage collector. Memory is reclaimed at statically known points — when a value's owner goes out of scope — so there is no background collector that periodically traverses the heap and, in doing so, competes with or pauses application threads.

For a service under load, the practical significance of this is concentrated in the tail of the latency distribution. Garbage-collected runtimes can deliver excellent median latency while still exhibiting occasional multi-millisecond or longer pauses when a collection cycle runs; these pauses are difficult to eliminate entirely and tend to appear precisely when allocation pressure is highest, which is often when the system is busiest. Because tail latency (for example the 99th or 99.9th percentile) frequently governs user-perceived responsiveness and the behavior of upstream timeouts and retries, the absence of GC pauses removes a significant and hard-to-predict source of tail variance. Rust does not make latency uniform by itself — allocator behavior, lock contention, and I/O still contribute — but it removes one large, non-deterministic contributor by construction.

A related benefit is memory footprint. Managed runtimes typically maintain headroom and metadata to support collection, and their resident set can fluctuate with the collector's state. Rust's deterministic reclamation yields a lower and more stable memory footprint, which improves the density of workloads that can be co-located on a host and makes capacity planning more predictable.

### 6.3 Throughput and energy efficiency

On sustained throughput, Rust is competitive with the fastest mainstream systems languages and substantially ahead of managed and interpreted ones. The most frequently cited independent evidence is the cross-language study by Pereira and colleagues, which measured execution time, energy consumption, and memory usage across a broad set of languages on a common benchmark suite. In that study Rust places among the most efficient languages, close to C, and well ahead of managed and interpreted languages on both time and energy [9]. The energy result is a direct corollary of the time result on this class of workload: energy consumed is largely a function of how long the processor is kept active to complete a unit of work, so a language that finishes sooner while doing comparable work generally draws less energy. For a backend operating at scale, this maps onto real operating cost — fewer machines, or the same machines doing more work, for the same power budget.

The following summarizes the qualitative positioning supported by the cited measurements; exact figures are workload-dependent and should be read from the source rather than treated as fixed constants.

| Property | Rust | C / C++ | Managed / interpreted |
|---|---|---|---|
| Execution time | Near the fastest [9] | Fastest [9] | Considerably slower [9] |
| Energy per task | Near-lowest [9] | Lowest [9] | Considerably higher [9] |
| Memory footprint | Low, deterministic | Low | Higher, variable |
| GC pause contribution to tail latency | None (no GC) | None (no GC) | Present |

### 6.4 Why predictability and efficiency matter under load

The value of these properties is most visible when a service is saturated rather than idle. Under load, three effects compound. First, predictable per-request cost makes the system's behavior tractable to reason about and to provision for: capacity models built on stable latency and footprint hold up as traffic grows, whereas models built on GC-influenced runtimes must account for pause-driven variance. Second, the elimination of GC pauses narrows the gap between median and tail latency, which reduces the incidence of timeout-triggered retries — retries that, once triggered, add load precisely when the system can least absorb it. Third, lower energy and memory cost per request translates into higher achievable density and lower marginal operating cost, which is a durable advantage for services that run continuously.

### 6.5 Limitations and honest scope

These advantages are structural, but they are not automatic. Performance always depends on implementation: an inefficient algorithm, an unnecessary allocation on a hot path, avoidable synchronization, or a poorly chosen data structure will dominate any language-level benefit. Rust's guarantees eliminate whole classes of pause and overhead; they do not substitute for measurement and profiling of the specific system in question. Benchmark results such as those in [9] describe a particular suite of workloads and hardware and should be read as indicative of relative positioning rather than as guarantees for any given service. Finally, deterministic memory management shifts certain costs to compile time and to the developer's design decisions — for instance, the discipline required to avoid unnecessary copying — rather than removing them entirely. The correct claim is therefore a measured one: Rust removes several of the largest and least predictable sources of runtime overhead, and it makes competitive throughput and low, stable resource usage achievable, while the realized performance of any particular backend remains a function of how it is built.
## 7. Correctness Engineering in Practice: How alma Uses the Type System

The preceding sections argued for Rust primarily on the grounds of memory safety, drawing on the industry evidence that a large majority of serious security vulnerabilities in systems software originate in memory-safety defects — approximately 70% of security-relevant CVEs assigned by the Microsoft Security Response Center [10] and a comparable share of the serious security bugs tracked in Chromium [16]. That argument, however, understates what Rust contributes to a codebase such as alma. Memory safety without garbage collection is Rust's foundational guarantee, formally established for the core language and its standard library abstractions by the RustBelt project [1] and articulated for a general engineering audience in *Safe Systems Programming in Rust* [2]. Beyond that foundation, Rust's ownership discipline, algebraic data types, and trait system can be used as instruments of *correctness engineering*: encoding domain and protocol invariants directly in types so that the compiler rejects incorrect programs before they run. This section grounds that claim in alma's actual implementation, showing four concrete techniques by which illegal states are made unrepresentable.

### 7.1 A type-state request pipeline

alma's HTTP layer models the lifecycle of an inbound request as a *type state* carried in a phantom type parameter. The central abstraction is `HttpRequestInPipeline<PipelineStage>`, whose stage marker is one of four uninhabited marker types — `RequestHasNotYetBeenValidated`, `RequestHasBeenValidated`, `RequestHasBeenAuthenticated`, and `RequestHasBeenAuthorized`. Because the markers are empty enums used only through `PhantomData`, they carry no runtime representation; the stage exists solely in the type checker.

Each transition is a method defined on exactly one stage that consumes `self` by value and returns the next stage:

| Method | Receiver stage | Result stage |
|---|---|---|
| `originate` | (constructor) | `RequestHasNotYetBeenValidated` |
| `validate` | `RequestHasNotYetBeenValidated` | `RequestHasBeenValidated` |
| `authenticate` | `RequestHasBeenValidated` | `RequestHasBeenAuthenticated` |
| `authorize` | `RequestHasBeenAuthenticated` | `RequestHasBeenAuthorized` |

The by-value receiver is essential: ownership transfer means the earlier-stage value is moved out and can no longer be referenced, so a request cannot be validated twice, nor can authorization be attempted on a request that was never authenticated. Accessors such as `authorized_principal` are defined *only* on `HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>`. A request handler that accepts this type is therefore statically guaranteed to receive a request that has already traversed validation, authentication, and authorization in order; the guarantee is enforced at compile time rather than by discipline or code review. An attempt to hand an unauthorized request to such a handler is not a bug that surfaces at runtime — it is a type error that fails to compile.

This construction leverages ownership for a purpose beyond memory management. The same move semantics that RustBelt models to prove the absence of use-after-free and data races [1][2] here prevent a request from being used in a stage it has not reached. It is worth stating the limitation plainly: type states enforce *ordering and presence*, not the correctness of each step's logic. The `authorize` transition still performs a runtime check that a principal is present, returning an `HttpError` when it is not; the type system guarantees the check is reached, not that any particular authorization policy is sound.

### 7.2 Validated value objects

alma's domain layer applies the same principle to data. The value objects `Email`, `NonEmptyText`, and `ProjectName` each wrap a private `String` and expose no public constructor other than a fallible `parse` associated function returning `Result<Self, DomainError>`. Because the inner field is private to the module, no code outside the constructor can fabricate an instance. Consequently, holding a value of one of these types is itself evidence that its invariant holds:

- `Email::parse` rejects empty input, requires exactly one `@` separator, requires non-empty local and domain parts, requires a `.` label separator in the domain, and normalizes the accepted value to lower case.
- `NonEmptyText::parse` rejects input that is empty after trimming.
- `ProjectName::parse` rejects empty names and names exceeding a fixed maximum length, trimming surrounding whitespace on the accepted value.

Validation is thereby pushed to the boundary and performed once. Downstream code that receives an `Email` need not — and cannot usefully — re-check its shape, which eliminates a class of defensive-programming inconsistencies in which the same value is validated differently, or not at all, at different call sites. The `serde::Deserialize` implementation for `Email` routes deserialization through the same `parse` function, so a malformed address arriving over the wire is rejected at the deserialization boundary and can never enter the domain as a constructed-but-invalid value. This pattern — parsing untrusted input into types that make the parsed invariant intrinsic — is a direct application of the safe-systems-programming philosophy Rust is designed to support [2].

### 7.3 Exhaustive error handling and a closed error taxonomy

alma performs error handling through `Result` and `Option` rather than exceptions or sentinel values, and the compiler's exhaustiveness checking on `match` ensures that every variant of an error enum is addressed. The HTTP error taxonomy `HttpError` is a closed enum with a fixed set of variants — malformed request body, missing authentication credentials, invalid authentication credentials, denied authorization, resource not found, and upstream application failure. Each variant maps deterministically to an HTTP status code and a stable machine-readable category label. Errors originating in the application layer are translated into this taxonomy through a `From<ApplicationError>` implementation, so the mapping from internal failure modes to client-visible responses is centralized and total. Adding a new failure mode forces the author to extend the relevant match arms, and the compiler flags every site that must be updated; there is no path by which an error is silently dropped or a status code left undefined.

### 7.4 Ports and adapters via traits

Finally, alma applies a ports-and-adapters (hexagonal) architecture in which the application layer depends only on trait abstractions — `ProjectRepository`, `StoragePort`, `DocumentCollectionPort`, `LiteraturePort`, `UnitOfWork`, and `ArtificialIntelligencePort`, among others — while concrete infrastructure implements those traits. The domain and application crates therefore have no compile-time dependency on any specific database, object store, or external service. This decoupling has two practical consequences. First, infrastructure can be substituted — for instance, replacing a live adapter with an in-memory test double — without altering domain logic, because the substitution is a change of the concrete type satisfying a trait bound. Second, the trait signatures act as an enforced contract: an adapter that fails to implement a required method, or implements it with a mismatched signature, does not compile. Combined with the value objects of §7.2, the ports carry validated domain types across the boundary — the `ProjectRepository` trait, for example, is defined in terms of `Email` and `ProjectId` rather than raw strings — so invariants are preserved as data crosses architectural seams.

Taken together, these four techniques illustrate that alma treats the type system not merely as a guardrail against memory-safety defects but as the primary medium for expressing and enforcing correctness. The memory-safety guarantees remain the load-bearing foundation, formally justified for the language itself [1] and consequential for security at industry scale [10][16]; the type-state pipeline, validated value objects, exhaustive error handling, and trait-based ports build on that foundation to move whole categories of logical error from runtime to compile time [2].
## 8. Empirical Evidence, Adoption, and Honest Trade-offs

The case for Rust cannot rest on formal guarantees alone. A language may be sound in principle yet fail in practice if developers routinely circumvent its guarantees, if its safety mechanisms address problems that rarely occur, or if the cost of adoption exceeds the value delivered. This section reviews the empirical record on how Rust behaves in real-world use, surveys the trajectory of industry adoption, and gives a candid accounting of the trade-offs that any adopting organization must weigh. The conclusion is measured rather than promotional: Rust carries real costs, but the evidence supports it as the appropriate foundation for alma.

### 8.1 What the empirical studies show

The most direct evidence comes from systematic studies of production Rust code. Qin et al. examined memory-safety and thread-safety bugs across a corpus of real-world Rust programs and their bug reports, and reported a consistent pattern: the large majority of memory-safety issues were connected to `unsafe` code, while the safe subset of the language largely delivered on its promise of preventing memory errors [5]. Their analysis of concurrency bugs further found that Rust's ownership and type discipline eliminated many classes of data race, though logic-level concurrency errors and deadlocks — which the type system does not claim to prevent — still occurred [5]. The practical implication is significant: the safety boundary in Rust is real and observable in the field, and defects concentrate at the points where that boundary is explicitly opted out of.

This raises the question of how `unsafe` is actually used. Astrauskas et al. studied unsafe usage across the crates.io ecosystem and found that `unsafe` blocks are comparatively rare, tend to be small, and are frequently used to interface with foreign code or to build safe abstractions over low-level operations rather than being spread indiscriminately through application logic [6]. This "unsafe is localized" finding matters for auditability: if unsoundness can only originate in a small, syntactically marked, and typically encapsulated fraction of the codebase, then security review can be focused where it yields the most value. Bae et al. reinforced the counterpoint that such code still demands scrutiny; their Rudra tooling found memory-safety bugs at ecosystem scale, including in widely used crates, demonstrating that unsafe code is a genuine and recurring source of defects that automated analysis can help surface [21].

Whether developers use Rust safely in practice has also been studied directly. Evans et al. analyzed public Rust code and observed that although unsafe usage exists, many developers avoid it entirely and often rely on well-vetted libraries to encapsulate the unsafe operations they do depend on [7]. The organizational and human dimension was examined by Fulton et al., who interviewed developers and teams adopting Rust [8]. Their findings are instructive because they are mixed. Participants consistently reported that once code compiled, they had higher confidence in its correctness and memory safety, and several noted a reduction in certain classes of runtime bug [8]. At the same time, they reported that the learning curve and the effort required to satisfy the compiler were the principal barriers, and that these costs were front-loaded and eased with experience [8]. The picture that emerges across [5], [6], [7], and [8] is coherent: Rust's guarantees hold up under real use, the danger is concentrated and manageable, and the primary cost is human rather than technical.

### 8.2 Industry adoption and developer sentiment

Adoption trends provide independent corroboration. Rust has moved from a research-adjacent language to a component of security-critical production systems across major organizations. Google reported integrating memory-safe languages, including Rust, into Android, and observed that as the proportion of memory-safe code rose, the proportion of memory-safety vulnerabilities fell correspondingly [11]; subsequent work articulated a "safe coding" strategy aimed at eliminating memory-safety vulnerabilities at the source by prioritizing memory-safe languages for new development [12]. This aligns with public guidance from government bodies: the NSA identified memory-safe languages, naming Rust among them, as a mitigation for the dominant class of software vulnerabilities [13]; CISA and international partners called for organizations to publish memory-safe roadmaps [14]; and the U.S. Office of the National Cyber Director urged a shift toward memory-safe languages as a national-scale software-security measure [15]. These positions are grounded in the underlying vulnerability data: Microsoft reported that approximately 70% of the CVEs it assigned over a multi-year period were memory-safety issues [10], and the Chromium project independently reported that roughly 70% of its serious security bugs are memory-safety bugs [16]. Rust directly targets this dominant defect class.

Developer sentiment has tracked this trajectory. The Stack Overflow Annual Developer Survey has ranked Rust as the most-admired or most-loved language repeatedly across successive years from 2016 through 2024 [17]. Sentiment is not a proof of technical merit, but sustained positive regard from practitioners who use a language daily is a meaningful signal that its benefits are perceived to outweigh its friction in practice.

### 8.3 An honest account of the trade-offs

Rust's costs are real and should not be minimized.

| Trade-off | Nature of the cost | Evidence / mitigating factor |
|---|---|---|
| Learning curve | Ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes require a genuine shift in mental model | Reported as the primary adoption barrier; front-loaded and eases with experience [8] |
| Compile times | The type and borrow checking that provide guarantees add build cost | Inherent to the design; affects iteration speed, partially offset by incremental compilation |
| Borrow-checker friction | Valid programs are sometimes rejected, requiring restructuring | Real short-term cost, but correlates with the higher post-compilation confidence developers report [8] |
| Ecosystem maturity | Some domains have less mature libraries than established languages | Improving with adoption [11][12], but must be assessed per domain |

Two further points warrant honesty. First, Rust does not eliminate all defect classes: it does not prevent logic errors, deadlocks, or resource leaks, and its safety guarantees can be suspended within `unsafe` blocks, which remain a demonstrated source of bugs [5][21]. Second, the runtime efficiency that Rust offers — it is consistently among the fastest and most energy-efficient languages in comparative benchmarks [9] — is a benefit rather than a cost, but it does not offset the human costs enumerated above; those must be paid regardless.

### 8.4 Verdict for alma

Weighing this evidence, Rust is the appropriate choice for alma. The dominant, most damaging, and most costly class of software vulnerability is memory-safety errors [10][16][13], and Rust addresses that class at the language level with guarantees that hold up under real-world scrutiny [5][6][7]. The principal costs — the learning curve, compile times, and borrow-checker friction — are front-loaded, one-time, and diminishing, whereas the benefit is a durable reduction in an entire category of security-critical defects over the system's lifetime [8][11][12]. Convergent guidance from security authorities [13][14][15] and broad, sustained adoption and developer regard [11][17] indicate that this trade is one an increasing share of serious engineering organizations is choosing to make. For a system where security and reliability are foundational requirements, accepting a bounded, front-loaded cost to obtain a lasting reduction in the most consequential defect class is a rational and defensible engineering decision.
