## 1. Preface

### 1.1 Why this document exists

This document exists because software that cannot be read cannot be trusted, and
software that can be read but not *understood in full* is merely trusted on faith.
The `alma-http` crate is the outermost adapter of a hexagonal system: it is the
membrane through which the untamed, entropic outside world — with its malformed
JSON, its absent headers, its lowercase-and-uppercase-confused email addresses —
is filtered, validated, authenticated, authorized, and finally permitted to speak
to an application core that has been engineered to assume nothing.

Most API references are terse. They tell you the path, the verb, the shape, and
they trust you to infer the rest. This reference does not extend you that
courtesy, and it does not extend it *by design*. Every guarantee the type system
makes, every invariant a value object enforces, every status code the error
taxonomy can emit, and every header the extractor consults is spelled out here in
full, at length, and without the merciful compression that a more restrained
author might have applied.

If you have arrived here looking for a quick answer, you will find it — but you
will have to wade through the surrounding rigor to reach it. That is the price of
a document that is complete.

### 1.2 How to read this document

Read it in order at least once. The sections are arranged so that each builds on
its predecessor:

1. **Preface** (you are here) establishes the tone, the notation, and the promise.
2. **Architecture Theory** gives you the mental model: the layers, the ports, the
   adapters, and the philosophical commitments that motivate the code.
3. **The Request Pipeline** describes the type-state machine that every request
   traverses, from an unvalidated correlation identifier to an authorized
   principal.
4. **Authentication Model** is reproduced verbatim from the design intent and
   should be treated as normative.
5. **Error Taxonomy** enumerates every way a request can fail at the HTTP boundary
   and exactly what the caller will see on the wire.
6. **Value Objects & Validation** documents the domain primitives — `Email`,
   `NonEmptyText`, `ProjectName` — with worked examples of what parses and what is
   rejected.
7. **Conventions** codifies naming, casing, pagination, and the format of the
   per-endpoint sections that follow this front matter.
8. **Route Macro** explains the `#[route(method, path)]` attribute that decorates
   every handler.

After the first linear read, treat the Table of Contents as your index. Every
subsequent visit can be a jump.

### 1.3 Scope and intent

**This document is comprehensive by design.** It is long, and it is repetitive where
repetition reinforces a guarantee. It restates in prose what the type system
already enforces in code, because the reader who understands *why* the compiler
rejects an unauthorized request is a reader who will not try to route around the
guarantee. The level of detail is intentional and is meant to provide a
complete, self-contained reference for implementers and integrators of this
API.

### 1.4 Notational conventions used throughout

- Fixed-width identifiers such as `HttpRequestInPipeline` refer to real Rust
  items in the codebase and can be grepped for verbatim.
- `← BUG` never appears in this reference; that marker is reserved for diagnostic
  diagrams elsewhere.
- ASCII diagrams are used in preference to rendered images so that this document
  remains legible in a terminal, a diff, and a code review alike.
- HTTP header names are written lowercase (`x-request-id`) because HTTP header
  names are case-insensitive and the codebase consults them in lowercase.

---

## 2. Architecture Theory

### 2.1 Hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters)

`alma-http` is one adapter in a hexagonal (ports-and-adapters) system. The
governing principle is the **Dependency Rule**: source-code dependencies point
*inward*, toward the domain, and never outward toward infrastructure. The domain
knows nothing of HTTP, of databases, of large language models, or of object
storage. It exposes *ports* — abstract capabilities expressed as traits — and the
outside world supplies *adapters* that implement those ports.

Concretely, the application core defines ports such as:

- `StoragePort` — the capability to persist and retrieve blobs.
- `ArtificialIntelligencePort` — the capability to consult a model.
- `LiteraturePort` — the capability to query bibliographic sources.
- `DocumentCollectionPort` — the capability to manage a corpus of documents.
- `UnitOfWork` — the capability to run a set of mutations transactionally.

The `alma-http` crate is a **driving adapter** (it drives the application inward,
in response to inbound requests). The concrete storage, AI, literature, and
persistence implementations are **driven adapters** (the application drives them
outward). The HTTP layer never names a concrete adapter; it holds only
`Arc<dyn Port>` trait objects, injected at the composition root.

### 2.2 Domain-Driven Design

The domain layer is populated with **value objects** — immutable, self-validating
types whose only public constructor is a fallible `parse` — and with strongly
typed identifiers (`ProjectId`, `UserId`, `CorpusId`, `VideoId`, and their phantom
markers) that make it impossible to pass a user identifier where a project
identifier is expected. A value object, once constructed, is *by construction*
valid; there is no code path that yields an `Email` that is not a well-formed
email, nor a `ProjectName` that is empty or oversized. Validation is not a step
that callers must remember to perform — it is the *only* way to obtain the type at
all.

### 2.3 CQRS and event sourcing

The application layer is organized around **use cases**, each annotated with the
`#[use_case(name = "...")]` attribute macro so that it carries a stable,
introspectable label. Use cases naturally partition into *commands* (which mutate
state and are executed inside a `UnitOfWork`) and *queries* (which do not), giving
the codebase a **CQRS**-shaped seam even where a full command/query bus is not
present. The `UnitOfWork` port is the transactional boundary: a command's
mutations either all commit or all roll back, which is the substrate on which an
**event-sourced** projection could be layered without disturbing the HTTP surface.
This reference describes the surface as it is; the event-sourcing story is stated
here as the architectural intent that the transactional boundary was chosen to
preserve.

### 2.4 The layer diagram

```
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                        bootstrap                               │
        │   composition root: constructs adapters, injects them into     │
        │   ApplicationState, mounts the complete router                 │
        └───────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                         │ owns / assembles
                                         ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                           http                                 │
        │   axum Router · #[route(...)] handlers · type-state pipeline   │
        │   RequestObservationLayer · RateLimitingLayer · HttpError      │
        └───────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                         │ calls inward via ports
                                         ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                        application                             │
        │   use cases (#[use_case]) · ports (traits) · ApplicationError  │
        │   StoragePort · AiPort · LiteraturePort · UnitOfWork · ...     │
        └───────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                         │ depends only on
                                         ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                          domain                                │
        │   value objects (Email, NonEmptyText, ProjectName) · typed Ids │
        │   invariants · DomainError · optics/prisms                     │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                         ▲
                                         │ implements ports (driven adapters)
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                       infrastructure                           │
        │   concrete StoragePort / AiPort / LiteraturePort / UnitOfWork  │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

        Dependency Rule: every arrow of *source dependency* points inward,
        toward domain. Infrastructure implements domain-facing ports; it is
        never named by the layers above it.
```

### 2.5 `ApplicationState`: the composition root

Every axum handler is given, through axum's `State` mechanism, a value of type
`ApplicationState<TransactionalUnitOfWork>`. This struct is the concrete embodiment
of the composition root — the single place where the abstract ports meet their
injected implementations. It is generic over the unit-of-work type so that tests
can substitute an in-memory transactional implementation while production supplies
a database-backed one. Its fields are exactly the five ports the application
needs:

```rust
pub struct ApplicationState<TransactionalUnitOfWork>
where
    TransactionalUnitOfWork: UnitOfWork,
{
    pub storage_adapter: Arc<dyn StoragePort>,
    pub artificial_intelligence_adapter: Arc<dyn ArtificialIntelligencePort>,
    pub literature_adapter: Arc<dyn LiteraturePort>,
    pub document_collection: Arc<dyn DocumentCollectionPort>,
    pub transactional_unit_of_work: Arc<TransactionalUnitOfWork>,
}
```

Because every field is an `Arc`, the struct is cheaply `Clone`, which is precisely
what axum requires of application state. The complete router is assembled by
`build_complete_router`, which merges twelve category sub-routers — projects,
project files, auth, AI, AI agents, OCR, literature, videos, RAG, community,
templates/policy, and docs — each parameterized over the same
`TransactionalUnitOfWork` type.

---

## 3. The Request Pipeline

### 3.1 The type-state machine

The central conceit of the HTTP layer is that **the progress of a request through
validation, authentication, and authorization is encoded in the type system**,
not in runtime flags. A request is represented by
`HttpRequestInPipeline<PipelineStage>`, where `PipelineStage` is one of four
uninhabited marker enums:

- `RequestHasNotYetBeenValidated`
- `RequestHasBeenValidated`
- `RequestHasBeenAuthenticated`
- `RequestHasBeenAuthorized`

These markers are *empty enums* (they have no variants and therefore no values);
they exist purely as `PhantomData` type parameters. The methods that advance the
pipeline are implemented **only** on the appropriate stage, so the compiler
enforces the ordering:

```
HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasNotYetBeenValidated>
        │  .originate(correlation_identifier: String)   (constructor)
        │  .validate()   -> Result<…Validated…, HttpError>
        ▼
HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenValidated>
        │  .authenticate(principal: Email) -> Result<…Authenticated…, HttpError>
        ▼
HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthenticated>
        │  .authorize() -> Result<…Authorized…, HttpError>
        ▼
HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>
        │  .correlation_identifier() -> &str
        │  .authorized_principal()   -> &Email
```

It is **impossible**, at compile time, to call `.authorize()` on a request that
has not been authenticated, or to read `.authorized_principal()` on a request that
has not been authorized. The accessor `authorized_principal()` contains an
`.expect(...)` that can never fire, because the only way to reach the
`RequestHasBeenAuthorized` state is through `.authorize()`, which returns
`AuthorizationWasDenied` unless a principal is present. The type-state design turns
a class of ordering bugs into compile errors.

- `.validate()` fails with `RequestBodyWasMalformed` if the correlation
  identifier is empty after trimming.
- `.authenticate(principal)` records the supplied `Email` as the declared
  principal and always succeeds at this stage.
- `.authorize()` fails with `AuthorizationWasDenied` if no principal is present;
  otherwise it produces the terminal authorized request.

### 3.2 The sequence of an inbound request

```
Client            axum Router        FromRequestParts          HttpRequestInPipeline<…>
  │                    │             (extractor)                        │
  │  HTTP request      │                    │                           │
  │───────────────────▶│                    │                           │
  │                    │  route match       │                           │
  │                    │───────────────────▶│                           │
  │                    │                    │ read x-request-id         │
  │                    │                    │   (default if absent)     │
  │                    │                    │ read x-account-email      │
  │                    │                    │   (401 if absent)         │
  │                    │                    │───── originate ──────────▶│  NotYetValidated
  │                    │                    │───── validate() ─────────▶│  Validated
  │                    │                    │───── authenticate() ─────▶│  Authenticated
  │                    │                    │───── authorize() ────────▶│  Authorized
  │                    │◀── Ok(authorized) ─│                           │
  │                    │  handler runs with authorized request + State  │
  │◀───── response ────│                    │                           │
```

If any stage returns an `HttpError`, the extractor short-circuits and that error
is converted into an HTTP response (see [Section 5](#5-error-taxonomy)); the
handler body never runs.

### 3.3 The extractor

The bridge from raw bytes to a type-safe authorized request is an axum
`FromRequestParts` implementation for
`HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>`. Its `Rejection` type is
`HttpError`, so a failed extraction is already a well-formed error response. The
extractor performs, in order:

1. **Resolve the correlation identifier** from the `x-request-id` header. If the
   header is absent or not valid text, it defaults to the literal
   `"unassigned-correlation-identifier"`. The correlation identifier is therefore
   *never* the cause of a rejection at the header-reading step (though an
   all-whitespace value would be rejected at `.validate()`).
2. **Resolve the authenticated account** from the `x-account-email` header. If the
   header is **absent**, the extractor returns
   `AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing`. If the header is present but not valid
   text (non-ASCII / non-UTF-8 bytes that fail `to_str`), it returns
   `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`.
3. **Parse the account into an `Email`** using the `email_string_prism()` optic's
   `.preview(...)`. If the raw value does not parse into a valid email, it returns
   `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`.
4. **Drive the type-state machine**: `originate → validate → authenticate →
   authorize`, propagating any `HttpError` with `?`.

Because the extractor yields the terminal `RequestHasBeenAuthorized` type, any
handler that takes that type as an argument is *guaranteed* by the compiler to run
only for requests that carried a valid, parsed principal.

### 3.4 The headers: `x-request-id` and `x-account-email`

| Header | Constant | Required? | On absence | On invalid |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `x-request-id` | `CORRELATION_IDENTIFIER_HEADER_NAME` | No | Defaults to `"unassigned-correlation-identifier"` | Treated as absent → default |
| `x-account-email` | `AUTHENTICATED_ACCOUNT_HEADER_NAME` | **Yes** | `401` `authentication_credentials_were_missing` | `401` `authentication_credentials_were_invalid` |

The `x-account-email` header is the sole carrier of identity at the HTTP boundary
(see the Authentication Model below). The `x-request-id` header exists to
correlate a single logical request across log lines and downstream systems; it is
observability infrastructure, not a security control.

### 3.5 Cross-cutting layers: observation and rate limiting

Two `tower` layers wrap handlers as cross-cutting concerns:

- **`RequestObservationLayer`** — a `tower::Layer`/`Service` pair that, on every
  `call`, emits a `tracing::info!` event recording the HTTP method and request
  path (`"an inbound request entered the observation middleware"`) before
  delegating to the inner service. It does not modify the request or response; it
  observes.

- **`RateLimitingLayer<const WINDOW_SECONDS: u64, const MAXIMUM_REQUESTS: u32>`** —
  a **fixed-window** limiter parameterized by const generics. It holds an
  `Arc<Mutex<FixedWindowState>>` tracking the window start instant and the count of
  requests observed in the current window. On each `call`: if the window has
  elapsed (`>= WINDOW_SECONDS`), the window resets; if the count has reached
  `MAXIMUM_REQUESTS`, the request is rejected with `429 Too Many Requests` and a
  plain-text body of the form `"rate limit of {MAXIMUM_REQUESTS} requests per
  {WINDOW_SECONDS} seconds exceeded"`; otherwise the count is incremented and the
  request proceeds. Note that this `429` body is *plain text*, not the JSON error
  envelope described in Section 5 — it is produced by the middleware before the
  handler and its error machinery are reached.

---

## 4. Authentication Model

Authentication in `alma-http` is **header-borne and trust-delegated**. The HTTP
layer does not verify passwords, validate JWT signatures, or terminate a session;
it *consumes an already-established identity* that an upstream trusted component —
a gateway, an authenticating reverse proxy, or the deployment's edge — has placed
into the `x-account-email` request header.

The model is as follows, and this section is normative:

1. **Identity is asserted by exactly one header: `x-account-email`.** Its value is
   the caller's email address in raw string form.

2. **Absence is unauthenticated.** If `x-account-email` is not present on the
   request, the extractor rejects with
   `AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing` (`HTTP 401`). There is no anonymous
   access path through the authorized extractor.

3. **Malformation is unauthenticated.** If the header is present but is not valid
   text, or if its text does not parse into a valid `Email` value object, the
   extractor rejects with `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid` (`HTTP 401`). A
   syntactically invalid identity is treated as no identity.

4. **A valid identity is a domain `Email`, not a string.** Once the header value
   passes the `email_string_prism()` optic, it exists in the pipeline as an
   `Email` value object — normalized, lowercased, and guaranteed well-formed — for
   the remainder of request handling.

5. **Authorization is a distinct, subsequent stage.** Authentication answers *who*
   the caller is; authorization answers *whether* they may proceed. In the current
   pipeline, `.authorize()` requires that a principal be present and, that
   condition met, admits the request; the seam exists so that richer, per-resource
   authorization policy can be introduced at exactly one place without altering the
   authentication contract above. Denied authorization surfaces as
   `AuthorizationWasDenied` (`HTTP 403`).

6. **The trust boundary is the deployment perimeter.** Because identity is
   delegated, `alma-http` **must not** be exposed to untrusted clients that can set
   `x-account-email` directly. It is the deployment's responsibility to strip any
   client-supplied `x-account-email` at the edge and to set it only after
   successful upstream authentication. This is the load-bearing assumption of the
   entire model.

---

## 5. Error Taxonomy

Every failure that the HTTP layer can express is one of six variants of a single
enum, and every one of those variants serializes to a single, stable JSON shape.
There is no other error envelope emitted by the handler machinery (the rate
limiter's `429` plain-text body noted in §3.5 is the sole documented exception,
because it originates in middleware before this machinery is reached).

### 5.1 The `HttpError` enumeration

```rust
pub enum HttpError {
    RequestBodyWasMalformed { explanation: String },
    AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing { explanation: String },
    AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid { explanation: String },
    AuthorizationWasDenied { explanation: String },
    RequestedResourceWasNotFound { explanation: String },
    UpstreamApplicationFailure { explanation: String },
}
```

Each variant carries a human-readable `explanation` string. `HttpError`
implements `IntoResponse`, so returning it from an extractor or a handler produces
a complete HTTP response directly.

### 5.2 The serialized wire body

Every `HttpError` is rendered to JSON via a private struct:

```rust
struct SerializedErrorBody {
    error_category: String,
    error_explanation: String,
}
```

- `error_category` is a stable, machine-readable snake_case label (the
  `category_label()` for the variant). Clients should branch on this field, not on
  the human-readable text.
- `error_explanation` is the variant's `explanation` string, intended for humans
  and logs. Its wording is **not** part of the stable contract and may change.

### 5.3 The complete status-code mapping table

| `HttpError` variant | `error_category` | HTTP status |
|---|---|---|
| `RequestBodyWasMalformed` | `request_body_was_malformed` | `400 Bad Request` |
| `AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing` | `authentication_credentials_were_missing` | `401 Unauthorized` |
| `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid` | `authentication_credentials_were_invalid` | `401 Unauthorized` |
| `AuthorizationWasDenied` | `authorization_was_denied` | `403 Forbidden` |
| `RequestedResourceWasNotFound` | `requested_resource_was_not_found` | `404 Not Found` |
| `UpstreamApplicationFailure` | `upstream_application_failure` | `500 Internal Server Error` |

### 5.4 Translation from `ApplicationError`

When a use case in the application layer fails, its `ApplicationError` is converted
into an `HttpError` via a `From` implementation, which performs the following
mapping:

| `ApplicationError` | Becomes `HttpError` | Resulting status |
|---|---|---|
| `RequestedProjectCouldNotBeLocated` | `RequestedResourceWasNotFound` | `404` |
| `RequestedResourceCouldNotBeLocated` | `RequestedResourceWasNotFound` | `404` |
| `AuthorizationWasDenied` | `AuthorizationWasDenied` | `403` |
| `DomainInvariantViolated(_)` | `RequestBodyWasMalformed` | `400` |
| *any other variant* | `UpstreamApplicationFailure` | `500` |

The `explanation` in each case is the `to_string()` of the originating application
error. Note the deliberate design choice: a **violated domain invariant** — for
example, an attempt to construct a value object from invalid input — is reported to
the caller as a `400`, because from the HTTP layer's perspective the *request* was
malformed; the domain merely refused to accept it.

### 5.5 Example error bodies

**Missing authentication header** — `HTTP 401`:

```json
{
  "error_category": "authentication_credentials_were_missing",
  "error_explanation": "the 'x-account-email' header was absent"
}
```

**Unparseable email in the account header** — `HTTP 401`:

```json
{
  "error_category": "authentication_credentials_were_invalid",
  "error_explanation": "the account header did not parse into a valid email address"
}
```

**Authorization denied** — `HTTP 403`:

```json
{
  "error_category": "authorization_was_denied",
  "error_explanation": "no authenticated principal was present at the authorization stage"
}
```

**Resource not found** — `HTTP 404`:

```json
{
  "error_category": "requested_resource_was_not_found",
  "error_explanation": "the requested project could not be located"
}
```

**Malformed request body / violated invariant** — `HTTP 400`:

```json
{
  "error_category": "request_body_was_malformed",
  "error_explanation": "the correlation identifier was empty"
}
```

**Upstream application failure** — `HTTP 500`:

```json
{
  "error_category": "upstream_application_failure",
  "error_explanation": "<the underlying application error, stringified>"
}
```

## 6. Value Objects & Validation

The domain layer refuses to hold invalid data. Each value object below has a
private field and a single fallible constructor named `parse` that returns
`Result<Self, DomainError>`. Each also implements `serde::Serialize` (as a plain
string) and `serde::Deserialize` (routing deserialization *through* `parse`, so
that every value arriving over the wire is validated at the boundary). Each
provides `as_str(&self) -> &str` and `into_string(self) -> String`.

### 6.1 `Email`

`Email` stores a single normalized representation and enforces a deliberately
strict, hand-written validation rather than a permissive regex.

**Rules, in the order they are checked:**

1. The candidate is trimmed of surrounding whitespace.
2. It must be **non-empty after trimming**.
3. It must contain **exactly one** `@` separator (zero or two or more is
   rejected, with the found count reported).
4. The **local part** (before `@`) must be non-empty.
5. The **domain part** (after `@`) must be non-empty.
6. The domain part must contain at least one `.` label separator.
7. On success, the value is stored **lowercased** (`to_ascii_lowercase`), so
   equality and hashing are case-insensitive with respect to ASCII.

**Valid examples:**

| Input | Stored as |
|---|---|
| `alice@example.com` | `alice@example.com` |
| `  Alice@Example.COM  ` | `alice@example.com` |
| `first.last@sub.domain.org` | `first.last@sub.domain.org` |

**Invalid examples (each yields `DomainError::EmailMalformed`):**

| Input | Reason |
|---|---|
| `` (empty / all whitespace) | value was empty after trimming |
| `plainaddress` | expected exactly one `@` but found 0 |
| `a@@b.com` | expected exactly one `@` but found 2 |
| `@example.com` | local part preceding `@` was empty |
| `alice@` | domain part following `@` was empty |
| `alice@localhost` | domain part did not contain a `.` label separator |

### 6.2 `NonEmptyText`

`NonEmptyText` is the minimal guarantee that a string carries at least one
non-whitespace character, while **preserving the original value verbatim**
(including surrounding whitespace).

**Rules:**

1. The candidate is checked with `trim().is_empty()`.
2. If it is empty after trimming, `DomainError::NonEmptyTextEmpty` is returned.
3. Otherwise, the **original, untrimmed** value is preserved as-is.

**Valid examples:** `"hello"`, `"  hello  "` (stored with its whitespace),
`"x"`, `"多语言文本"`.

**Invalid examples (yield `DomainError::NonEmptyTextEmpty`):** `""`, `"   "`,
`"\t\n"`.

Contrast with `ProjectName`: `NonEmptyText` **does not trim** the stored value,
whereas `ProjectName` does.

### 6.3 `ProjectName`

`ProjectName` is a trimmed, length-bounded name for a project. The bound is the
public constant `PROJECT_NAME_MAXIMUM_LENGTH = 200`, measured in **Unicode scalar
values** (`chars().count()`), not bytes.

**Rules, in order:**

1. The candidate is trimmed.
2. It must be non-empty after trimming, else `DomainError::ProjectNameEmpty`.
3. Its `char` count must not exceed `200`, else
   `DomainError::ProjectNameTooLong { maximum: 200 }`.
4. On success, the **trimmed** value is stored canonically.

**Valid examples:**

| Input | Stored as |
|---|---|
| `My Thesis` | `My Thesis` |
| `  Draft 2  ` | `Draft 2` |
| a 200-character name | the same 200 characters |

**Invalid examples:**

| Input | Error |
|---|---|
| `""` / `"   "` | `ProjectNameEmpty` |
| a 201-character name | `ProjectNameTooLong { maximum: 200 }` |

---

## 7. Conventions

### 7.1 Naming: verbose to the point of confrontation

This codebase names things in full. Identifiers such as
`artificial_intelligence_adapter`, `HttpRequestInPipeline`,
`RequestHasNotYetBeenValidated`, `requests_observed_in_current_window`, and
`corresponding_status_code` are not abbreviated. The convention is that a name
should read as an English phrase and require no gloss. This reference honors that
convention when quoting the code; you should too when extending it. Terseness is
not prized here — clarity is.

### 7.2 JSON casing

- **Wire JSON field names are `snake_case`.** The canonical example is the error
  body: `error_category` and `error_explanation`. Request and response schemas in
  the per-endpoint sections follow the same convention unless a section explicitly
  states otherwise.
- **Value objects serialize as bare JSON strings**, not as objects. An `Email`
  appears on the wire as `"alice@example.com"`, never as
  `{"normalized_representation": "..."}`. The same holds for `NonEmptyText` and
  `ProjectName`.
- **Deserialization validates.** Because each value object's `Deserialize` routes
  through `parse`, a request body containing an invalid `Email` or an empty
  `ProjectName` fails deserialization, which surfaces as a `400`-class malformed
  request rather than reaching the handler.

### 7.3 Pagination

Where an endpoint returns a collection that may be large, the convention is
**offset/limit** query parameters, expressed in `snake_case`:

- `limit` — the maximum number of items to return; endpoints define a default and
  a hard ceiling, both stated in the endpoint's own section.
- `offset` — the number of items to skip from the start of the ordered result.

Responses to paginated endpoints wrap their items alongside enough metadata to
request the next page. Each per-endpoint section states the exact response shape;
where a section is silent on pagination, the endpoint returns its full result set
and pagination does not apply.

### 7.4 How to read the per-endpoint schema sections

Every endpoint documented after this front matter follows one fixed template. Read
each field of the template as follows:

- **Method & Path** — the HTTP verb and route, exactly as declared in the handler's
  `#[route(method = "...", path = "...")]` attribute (see Section 8). The path may
  contain axum path parameters written `:name`.
- **Authentication** — whether the endpoint uses the authorized-request extractor.
  Endpoints that take `HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>` require a
  valid `x-account-email` and will `401`/`403` per Sections 4 and 5 before the body
  runs.
- **Path / Query parameters** — name, type, whether required, and validation notes,
  including the value object each parameter parses into.
- **Request body** — the JSON schema, with `snake_case` fields and value-object
  string encodings as described in §7.2.
- **Responses** — the success status and body schema, followed by the applicable
  error categories drawn from the taxonomy in Section 5. Assume the full error
  taxonomy is reachable; each section highlights only the endpoint-specific ones.

---

## 8. Route Macro

Handlers are decorated with the attribute macro `#[route(method = "...", path =
"...")]`, defined in the `alma-macros` crate. Its job is deliberately small and
transparent: it attaches a **route descriptor** to each handler so that a
handler's verb and path live *next to the handler itself*, rather than in a distant
router-registration table.

Given a handler:

```rust
#[route(method = "POST", path = "/projects")]
async fn create_project(/* ... */) -> /* ... */ { /* ... */ }
```

the macro:

1. **Re-emits the annotated function unchanged.** The handler's own body and
   signature are untouched; the macro is purely additive.
2. **Generates a sibling descriptor function** named by suffixing the handler's
   identifier with `_route_descriptor` — here, `create_project_route_descriptor`.
   That function returns a `(&'static str, &'static str)` tuple of `(method,
   path)`, e.g. `("POST", "/projects")`.
3. **Applies defaults** for either argument that is omitted: the method defaults to
   `"GET"` and the path defaults to `"/"`. Arguments are parsed as
   `name = "string-literal"` pairs, in any order; unrecognized names are ignored.

The descriptor function is what the category router-builders consult when wiring a
handler into the axum `Router`, guaranteeing that the verb and path used at
registration are exactly the ones declared on the handler. There is no second
source of truth to drift out of sync.

> A companion macro, `#[use_case(name = "...")]`, applies the same philosophy to
> application-layer use-case structs: it re-emits the struct unchanged and attaches
> a `use_case_label() -> &'static str` associated function returning the configured
> name (defaulting to `"unnamed-use-case"`). It is documented here only for
> symmetry; it is not part of the HTTP surface.

---

*End of front matter. The per-endpoint reference sections follow.*

# Part II — Endpoint Reference



## Authentication & Session Category

| Method + Path | Endpoint |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/rate-limit/check` — Rate-Limit Quota Introspection | `check_rate_limit_quota` |
| `GET /api/auth/*nextauth_action` — NextAuth GET Action Compatibility Shim | `handle_nextauth_action_via_get` |
| `POST /api/auth/*nextauth_action` — NextAuth Catch-All Action Dispatcher (POST) | `handle_nextauth_action_via_post` |
| `GET /api/allowed-emails` — List the Application Access Allow-List | `list_allowed_emails` |
| `GET /api/debug-oauth-scopes` — Report the OAuth Scopes Granted to the Authenticated Principal | `list_oauth_scopes` |
| `GET /api/auth/session` — Retrieve the Authenticated Session Descriptor | `retrieve_authenticated_session` |
| `POST /api/auth/refresh-token` — Rotate the Caller's Refresh Token | `rotate_refresh_token` |

### `GET /api/rate-limit/check` — Rate-Limit Quota Introspection

#### Synopsis

This endpoint reports the authenticated principal's current standing against the per-window request quota without consuming any of that quota itself. It reads (never writes) the counter document for the caller's fixed 60-second window, computes the remaining allowance out of the 100-request budget, and returns a compact status report describing how many requests remain, how long the window is, and how many seconds remain until the window rolls over. If the caller has already exhausted the window's allowance the endpoint refuses with an authorization denial rather than returning a report.

#### Theory & Rationale

From a REST standpoint this is a canonical **safe, idempotent read**. `GET /api/rate-limit/check` is a pure projection over server-side state: invoking it once, twice, or a thousand times in the same window yields the same logical answer (modulo the monotonic march of `seconds_until_reset` and any writes performed by *other* endpoints) and mutates nothing. The handler never increments the consumed counter, never persists a document, and holds no transaction open for writing — it merely *fetches* the counter document and derives a view. This is the platonic ideal of an introspection resource: the client asks "where do I stand?" and the server answers truthfully without the observation perturbing the observed. Consequently it is freely retryable, freely cacheable-at-your-own-peril (the answer is time-sensitive), and carries no `If-Match`/optimistic-concurrency ceremony because there is nothing to concurrently clobber.

Within a Domain-Driven Design layering, this handler sits squarely in the **HTTP adapter (interface) layer** of the `auth` bounded context. It orchestrates domain and application concerns but owns no business rules of its own beyond the quota policy constants: the identity is a first-class domain `Email` value object (re-parsed at the boundary as a defensive measure), and persistence is reached exclusively through the `DocumentCollectionPort` application port, keeping the handler ignorant of the concrete counter store. The counters deliberately cohabit the `allowed_emails` document collection — the same collection that houses the identity records which grant authorization — so that a principal's quota lives physically next to the identity that legitimises it. The window arithmetic (fixed, contiguous, floored windows) is expressed as small, individually-tested pure functions, an intentional nod to functional-core / imperative-shell discipline: the shell (the async handler) does I/O, the core (the arithmetic helpers) is deterministic and trivially unit-testable.

#### Authentication & Required Headers

This endpoint is terminal in the type-state pipeline: the handler's argument is `HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>`, meaning the request must have already been **validated**, **authenticated**, and **authorized** by the upstream middleware before this function is ever entered. The authenticated principal's email is the sole input that keys the rate-limit counter.

| Header | Required | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x-account-email` | Yes | `x-account-email: researcher@example.com` | The caller's account email. This is the principal that the pipeline authenticates and authorizes, and it becomes the rate-limit subject. It is re-parsed inside the handler into a strongly-typed `Email`; a malformed value yields `401 AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`. |
| `x-request-id` | Recommended | `x-request-id: 7c3a1f2e-9b40-4d1a-8f22-0a1b2c3d4e5f` | Correlation identifier echoed through logs/traces for this request. Not consumed by this handler's business logic, but strongly recommended for observability and for correlating a quota check with the request that prompted it. |

**The type-state pipeline (`Validated -> Authenticated -> Authorized`), verbatim.** The alma-http framework threads every request through a compile-time state machine encoded in the type parameter of `HttpRequestInPipeline<S>`. A request first enters as **Validated**: its shape, headers, and basic well-formedness have been checked, but no identity has been established. It is then promoted to **Authenticated**: the credentials carried in `x-account-email` (and whatever the auth middleware consults) have been verified to correspond to a real, known principal — a failure here is where `AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing` / `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid` originate. Finally it becomes **Authorized**: the authenticated principal has been checked against the policy governing *this* resource, and only a request bearing the `RequestHasBeenAuthorized` marker is permitted to be handed to this handler — a failure at this stage produces `AuthorizationWasDenied`. Because the handler's signature demands `HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>`, it is *structurally impossible* to invoke this handler with a request that has not traversed all three stages; the compiler, not a runtime `if`, enforces the ordering. The handler then calls `authorized_request.authorized_principal()` to obtain the identity that survived authorization.

#### Path & Query Parameters

None.

The handler declares no path segments beyond the static `/api/rate-limit/check` and reads no query string whatsoever. The window size (60 s) and per-window allowance (100) are compile-time defaults, not client-tunable parameters.

#### Request Body

This is a `GET` request and the handler reads **no request body**. It extracts everything it needs from the authorized pipeline state (the principal's email) and from server-side configuration and clock. Any body sent by the client is ignored.

Field table (there are no body fields):

| Field | Type | Required | Constraints | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| _(none)_ | — | — | — | — | This endpoint reads no request body. |

#### Successful Response

On success the handler returns `200 OK` with a JSON object assembled by `serialize_rate_limit_quota_report`.

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `status` | string | Coarse status label. One of `"within_limits"` (more than 10 requests remain), `"approaching_limit"` (1–10 remain), or `"quota_exhausted"` (0 remain, though in practice an exhausted quota returns a 403 before this body is produced). |
| `remaining_requests` | integer (u32) | Requests still available in the current window, computed as `allowed - consumed`, saturating at zero. |
| `window_seconds` | integer (u64) | The fixed length of the rate-limit window, currently `60`. |
| `seconds_until_reset` | integer (u64) | Seconds remaining until the current window ends and the allowance resets; `0` if the window has already elapsed or the window length is zero. |

```json
  },
```

```json
}
```

#### Error Responses

Every error is serialized as a `SerializedErrorBody` with an `error_category` and an `error_explanation`.

| Status | error_category | When (for THIS endpoint) | Example body |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400 | `RequestBodyWasMalformed` | Not produced by this handler directly (it reads no body). Included for completeness; only reachable if upstream framework extraction rejects the request shape. | `{"error_category":"RequestBodyWasMalformed","error_explanation":"the request body could not be parsed"}` |
| 401 | `AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing` | Emitted upstream when no authenticating identity (`x-account-email`) is present; the request never reaches `RequestHasBeenAuthorized`. | `{"error_category":"AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing","error_explanation":"no authentication credentials were provided"}` |
| 401 | `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid` | Raised inside `parse_rate_limit_subject_as_email` when the authorized principal's identifier fails `Email::parse` (a malformed email leaking into the counter key). | `{"error_category":"AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid","error_explanation":"email address is not valid"}` |
| 403 | `AuthorizationWasDenied` | Raised by `reject_when_quota_exhausted` when `remaining_allowance == 0`; the explanation includes the retry countdown. Also produced upstream if the principal is not authorized for the resource. | `{"error_category":"AuthorizationWasDenied","error_explanation":"rate limit quota exhausted; retry in 42 second(s)"}` |
| 404 | `RequestedResourceWasNotFound` | Not produced for a missing counter document (a lookup miss is treated as zero consumption). Only reachable if the document-collection port returns `RequestedResourceCouldNotBeLocated`, which `map_document_collection_failure_to_http_error` defers to the canonical `From` conversion. | `{"error_category":"RequestedResourceWasNotFound","error_explanation":"the requested resource could not be located"}` |
| 500 | `UpstreamApplicationFailure` | Raised by `map_document_collection_failure_to_http_error` when the counter store reports a `DocumentCollectionFailure` (e.g. connection reset) while fetching the counter document. | `{"error_category":"UpstreamApplicationFailure","error_explanation":"the rate-limit counter store reported a failure: connection reset"}` |

One full `SerializedErrorBody` example (the most endpoint-specific case, quota exhaustion):

```json
{
  "error_category": "AuthorizationWasDenied",
  "error_explanation": "rate limit quota exhausted; retry in 42 second(s)"
}
```

#### Internal Processing Pipeline

The handler `check_rate_limit_quota_handler` executes the following real helper functions, in order:

1. `extract_rate_limit_subject_identifier(&authorized_request)` — pulls the authorized principal's email string out of the pipeline via `authorized_principal().as_str()`.
2. `parse_rate_limit_subject_as_email(subject_identifier)` — re-parses that string into a domain `Email`, mapping a parse failure to `401 AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`.
3. `default_requests_allowed_per_window()` — returns the per-window allowance constant, `100`.
4. `default_rate_limit_window_duration_seconds()` — returns the window length constant, `60` seconds.
5. `read_current_epoch_seconds()` — reads the system clock as epoch seconds, clamping a pre-epoch clock to `0`.
6. `compute_current_window_start_epoch_seconds(now, window_seconds)` — floors `now` to the start of its fixed window (or returns `now` when the window is zero).
7. `build_rate_limit_counter_document_key(&subject_email, window_start)` — builds the deterministic key `rate-limit::<email>::<window_start>`.
8. `load_consumed_request_count_for_window(&document_collection, &counter_key)` — fetches the counter document from the `allowed_emails` collection; a missing document means zero consumed.
   - internally calls `parse_consumed_count_from_counter_document_body(&body)` — reads `consumed_requests`, treating missing/negative/non-numeric as `0` and clamping oversized values to `u32::MAX`.
   - internally calls `map_document_collection_failure_to_http_error(err)` on port failure — maps `DocumentCollectionFailure` to `500 UpstreamApplicationFailure`, deferring other errors to the canonical `From`.
9. `compute_remaining_request_allowance(requests_allowed, requests_consumed)` — computes remaining allowance, saturating at zero.
10. `compute_seconds_until_window_reset(now, window_start, window_seconds)` — computes seconds until the window rolls over, saturating at zero for clock skew or zero-length windows.
11. `reject_when_quota_exhausted(remaining_allowance, seconds_until_reset)` — short-circuits with `403 AuthorizationWasDenied` (including the retry countdown) when zero allowance remains.
12. `is_request_within_configured_limits(requests_consumed, requests_allowed)` — authoritative boundary check backing the status label.
13. `determine_quota_status_label(remaining_allowance)` — maps the remaining allowance to `within_limits` / `approaching_limit` / `quota_exhausted`.
14. `serialize_rate_limit_quota_report(status_label, remaining_allowance, window_seconds, seconds_until_reset)` — assembles the final JSON body returned to the client.

#### Edge Cases & Gotchas

- **This check does not consume quota.** The handler only *reads* the counter document; it never increments `consumed_requests`. Some other endpoint is responsible for writing the counter. Polling `/api/rate-limit/check` in a tight loop will not exhaust your own quota (though it may hammer the document store).
- **A missing counter document is not a 404.** If no document exists for the subject/window key, `load_consumed_request_count_for_window` returns `0` (unseen this window), not `RequestedResourceWasNotFound`. A 404 only surfaces if the port itself signals `RequestedResourceCouldNotBeLocated`.
- **Corrupt counters silently read as zero (or clamp).** `parse_consumed_count_from_counter_document_body` treats a missing field, a string, a negative number, or non-numeric junk as `0`, and clamps values above `u32::MAX` down to `u32::MAX`. A poisoned document can therefore make a subject look fully unused rather than crashing the handler — fail-open, by design.
- **Windows are fixed and floored, not sliding.** The window start is `now` floored to a multiple of 60 seconds. Two requests one second apart but straddling a 60-second boundary land in different counter documents. `seconds_until_reset` is measured to the fixed window end, so it counts down toward a wall-clock-aligned reset, not a per-caller rolling one.
- **Clock skew and a zero-length window both collapse to an immediate reset.** `compute_seconds_until_window_reset` uses `saturating_sub`, so if `now` has already passed the computed window end, or if the window length were ever `0`, it reports `0` seconds until reset rather than underflowing.
- **`status` and the 403 can disagree in principle, but not in practice.** When allowance is exactly `0`, `reject_when_quota_exhausted` returns `403` *before* the status label is computed, so callers never actually observe a `200` body carrying `"status": "quota_exhausted"` from this path; the `quota_exhausted` branch of `determine_quota_status_label` is effectively unreachable on success.
- **The principal is re-parsed even though it was already authorized.** `parse_rate_limit_subject_as_email` re-validates the already-authorized email as a defensive guard against a malformed identifier contaminating the counter key — a belt-and-suspenders `401` that should essentially never fire in normal operation.

#### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Can I change the window size or the request limit via a query parameter or header?**
A: No. `default_requests_allowed_per_window()` returns `100` and `default_rate_limit_window_duration_seconds()` returns `60` as compile-time constants. There is no client-facing knob. Recompile, or take it up with whoever owns the constants.

**Q: If I call this endpoint 200 times, will I be rate-limited by my own polling?**
A: Not by this handler. It performs no write and increments no counter. Whether some *upstream* middleware counts this GET against you is a separate question this handler cannot answer; from its own perspective, checking your quota is free.

**Q: Why does an exhausted quota return `403 AuthorizationWasDenied` instead of the customary `429 Too Many Requests`?**
A: Because the handler models quota exhaustion as an authorization decision within the type-state pipeline, and its error taxonomy has no `429` variant — the closest and semantically-chosen fit is `AuthorizationWasDenied`, whose explanation string carries the `retry in N second(s)` countdown for you to honour.

### `GET /api/auth/*nextauth_action` — NextAuth GET Action Compatibility Shim

#### Synopsis

This endpoint is a catch-all, wildcard-routed compatibility shim that answers the read-style ("GET") family of NextAuth actions — `csrf`, `providers`, `session`, `signin` (with an optional trailing provider identifier), and `signout` — behind a single axum route. It normalizes an arbitrarily-shaped trailing path (`/api/auth/*nextauth_action`), classifies its leading segment into a known action kind, and returns a deterministic JSON envelope describing what NextAuth would have done. It reads **no request body**, consults **no authentication headers**, and touches **no upstream service or datastore**; every response it produces is synthesized purely from the shape of the path.

#### Theory & Rationale

In strict REST terms this endpoint is the platonic ideal of a **safe** and **idempotent** verb: it is a `GET`, it mutates nothing, it holds no lock, it acquires no unit-of-work transaction, and calling it once is observationally indistinguishable from calling it ten thousand times. The wildcard capture (`*nextauth_action`) exists precisely because NextAuth's client library treats `/api/auth/...` as an opaque namespace of sub-actions rather than a set of individually-declared routes; rather than enumerate `csrf`, `providers`, `session`, `signin`, `signin/:provider`, and `signout` as five-plus discrete axum routes, the design collapses them into one wildcard handler that performs its own in-band segment classification. This is a deliberate concession to an external contract (NextAuth's URL grammar) rather than an expression of our own domain.

From a Domain-Driven Design vantage point, it is worth being honest about placement: this handler lives in the `auth` HTTP category but it is almost entirely a **presentation/anti-corruption concern**, not a domain operation. The only place a domain value object surfaces is the validation of the optional `signin/:provider` trailing segment, which is parsed through `NonEmptyText` — the domain's minimal "this string is not blank" invariant. No aggregate is loaded, no repository is queried, no unit of work is opened. The endpoint therefore sits at the outermost ring of the hexagon: it adapts an inbound protocol shape into a canned response and defers absolutely nothing to the application layer. Treat it as a shim, document it as a shim, and do not mistake its `auth` folder for evidence that it authenticates anyone.

#### Authentication & Required Headers

This endpoint performs **no authentication and no authorization**. It does not extract, read, or validate any header. The handler signature accepts only `State(_application_state)` (bound but unused — note the leading underscore) and `Path(nextauth_action)`. The two conventional Alma request headers are therefore documented here for consistency with the rest of the API surface, but are **not consulted by this handler**:

| Header | Required | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x-request-id` | No (not read by this handler) | `x-request-id: 6f9619ff-8b86-d011-b42d-00cf4fc964ff` | Conventionally used for request correlation/tracing across the fleet. This handler never reads it; supply it anyway for log correlation upstream. |
| `x-account-email` | No (not read by this handler) | `x-account-email: user@example.com` | Conventionally carries the caller's principal for authenticated endpoints. This handler ignores it entirely — even the `session` probe reports `anonymous` because the GET path invokes `build_session_probe_response_body(None)` unconditionally. |

**Type-state pipeline (Validated → Authenticated → Authorized).** Elsewhere in the Alma HTTP layer, a request is conventionally advanced through a compile-time type-state pipeline: a raw request is first proven **Validated** (its shape/body parsed into domain value objects so that malformed input is unrepresentable past this stage), then **Authenticated** (a principal is extracted and proven, typically from `x-account-email`, yielding a token type that only exists once identity is established), then **Authorized** (a policy check consumes the authenticated token and produces an authorization token required to reach the protected operation). Each arrow is a distinct Rust type, so a handler that requires an `Authorized` token literally cannot be called with an unauthenticated request — the illegal state does not typecheck. **This particular endpoint stops at the first stage.** It performs a lightweight *Validated*-style step (normalizing and classifying the path, and parsing the optional provider through `NonEmptyText`) and then deliberately does **not** advance to *Authenticated* or *Authorized*. There is no principal extraction and no policy gate; the pipeline is truncated by design because the NextAuth read actions are public.

#### Path & Query Parameters

| Name | In | Type | Required | Constraints | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `nextauth_action` | path (wildcard `*`) | `String` | Yes | Everything after `/api/auth/` is captured. After normalization (trim, strip outer `/`, lowercase) it must be non-empty, and its leading `/`-delimited segment must be one of `csrf`, `providers`, `session`, `signin`, `signout`. | — | The NextAuth action to service. May include a trailing provider segment for sign-in, e.g. `signin/google`. Doubled slashes collapse; surrounding whitespace and casing are ignored. |

No query parameters are read by this handler.

#### Request Body

This endpoint reads **no request body**. It is a `GET` handler with the signature `(State(_application_state), Path(nextauth_action)) -> Result<Json<Value>, HttpError>`; there is no `Json<T>` / body extractor of any kind. Any bytes sent in the request body are ignored.

Field table (there are no body fields): **None.**

Empty-object JSON Schema (the accepted request body is the empty object — i.e. nothing):

```json

  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "HandleNextAuthActionViaGetRequestBody",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {},
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "description": "This GET endpoint reads no request body."
}
```

```typescript

```

```rust
//   Path(nextauth_action): Path<String>
```


#### Successful Response

**Status:** `200 OK`, `Content-Type: application/json`. The body is a free-form `serde_json::Value` object whose exact shape depends on the classified action kind. The stable, always-present fields are `action` and `http_method`; the remaining fields vary per action.

Response field table (union across all action kinds):

| Field | Type | Present for | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `action` | string | all | The canonical action name: `csrf`, `providers`, `session`, `signin`, `signout`, or `unknown`. |
| `http_method` | string | all | Always `"GET"`. |
| `status` | string | csrf / providers / signin / signout / unknown | Action outcome marker: `issued`, `handled`, `redirecting`, `signin_page`, `signed_out`, or `handled`. |
| `csrf_token` | string | csrf | Placeholder CSRF token (`"nextauth-csrf-placeholder-token"`). |
| `providers` | object | providers | Map of provider id → provider descriptor (`id`, `name`, `type`, `signin_url`, `callback_url`). Currently only `google`. |
| `session_status` | string | session | Always `"anonymous"` on the GET path (the handler passes `None` as the principal). |
| `authenticated_principal` | string \| null | session | Always `null` on the GET path. |
| `provider` | string \| null | signin | The validated provider id when `signin/:provider` was supplied; `null` for a bare `signin`. |
| `redirect_url` | string | signin (with provider) / signout | The NextAuth-style redirect target, e.g. `/api/auth/callback/google` or `/api/auth/signin`. |

JSON Schema for the success body (draft 2020-12):

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "HandleNextAuthActionViaGetResponse",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["action", "http_method"],
  "properties": {
    "action": {
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["csrf", "providers", "session", "signin", "signout", "unknown"]
    },
    "http_method": { "type": "string", "const": "GET" },
    "status": { "type": "string" },
    "csrf_token": { "type": "string" },
    "providers": { "type": "object", "additionalProperties": true },
    "session_status": { "type": "string", "enum": ["active", "anonymous"] },
    "authenticated_principal": { "type": ["string", "null"] },
    "provider": { "type": ["string", "null"] },
    "redirect_url": { "type": "string" }
  },
  "additionalProperties": true
}
```

Realistic `200 OK` example (`GET /api/auth/signin/google`):

```json
{
  "action": "signin",
  "http_method": "GET",
  "provider": "google",
  "redirect_url": "/api/auth/callback/google",
  "status": "redirecting"
}
```

#### Error Responses

Every `HttpError` variant serializes through `IntoResponse` into a `SerializedErrorBody` of exactly two fields: `error_category` and `error_explanation`. The table below lists every variant of the shared enum; the **When** column states whether and how *this specific handler* can produce it.

| Status | error_category | When (for THIS endpoint) | Example body |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400 | `request_body_was_malformed` | Only reachable via the `signin/:provider` branch: a provider segment that is present but blank/whitespace fails `NonEmptyText::parse`, mapped by `map_domain_error_to_malformed_action_error`. (Note: an empty second segment is normally dropped by `split_...`/`extract_...`, so this is a narrow edge.) | `{"error_category":"request_body_was_malformed","error_explanation":"non-empty text was empty"}` |
| 401 | `authentication_credentials_were_missing` | **Never** emitted by this handler — it performs no authentication. Listed for enum completeness. | `{"error_category":"authentication_credentials_were_missing","error_explanation":"..."}` |
| 401 | `authentication_credentials_were_invalid` | **Never** emitted by this handler — it performs no authentication. Listed for enum completeness. | `{"error_category":"authentication_credentials_were_invalid","error_explanation":"..."}` |
| 403 | `authorization_was_denied` | **Never** emitted by this handler — it performs no authorization. Listed for enum completeness. | `{"error_category":"authorization_was_denied","error_explanation":"..."}` |
| 404 | `requested_resource_was_not_found` | The normalized action is empty (`reject_empty_nextauth_action`), or the leading segment is not one of the five recognized actions (`reject_unknown_nextauth_action`). | `{"error_category":"requested_resource_was_not_found","error_explanation":"unsupported NextAuth GET action: 'callback'"}` |
| 500 | `upstream_application_failure` | **Never** emitted by this handler — it calls no upstream/application service. Listed for enum completeness. | `{"error_category":"upstream_application_failure","error_explanation":"..."}` |

Full `SerializedErrorBody` example (a real 404 from this endpoint):

```json
{
  "error_category": "requested_resource_was_not_found",
  "error_explanation": "unsupported NextAuth GET action: 'callback'"
}
```

#### Internal Processing Pipeline

The handler calls the following real helper functions, in order:

1. `normalize_nextauth_action_path_segment(nextauth_action)` — trims whitespace, strips leading/trailing `/`, and lowercases the raw wildcard capture into a canonical action string.
2. `reject_empty_nextauth_action(&normalized_action)` — returns `404 RequestedResourceWasNotFound` if normalization collapsed the path to an empty string.
3. `split_nextauth_action_into_segments(&normalized_action)` — splits on `/`, trims each piece, and discards empty segments (so `signin//github` → `["signin","github"]`).
4. `classify_nextauth_get_action(&action_segments)` — maps the leading segment to a `NextAuthGetActionKind` (`csrf`/`providers`/`session`/`signin`/`signout`, else `Unrecognized`).
5. `reject_unknown_nextauth_action(&action_kind, &normalized_action)` — returns `404 RequestedResourceWasNotFound` for `Unrecognized`; internally delegates to `is_recognized_nextauth_get_action`.
6. `extract_provider_identifier_from_signin_action(&action_segments)` — (only for `SignIn`) pulls the optional second segment as a provider candidate, or `None` for a bare `signin`.
7. `parse_provider_identifier_as_non_empty(provider_candidate)` — (only when a provider candidate exists) validates it via `NonEmptyText::parse`, converting failures through `map_domain_error_to_malformed_action_error` into `400 RequestBodyWasMalformed`.
8. `render_response_for_nextauth_get_action(&action_kind, &action_segments)` — the total dispatch function that builds the final `Value`, delegating to `build_csrf_token_response_body`, `build_providers_catalog_response_body`, `build_session_probe_response_body(None)`, `build_signin_redirect_response_body`, or `build_signout_confirmation_response_body`.

#### Edge Cases & Gotchas

- **The `session` GET action is always anonymous.** `render_response_for_nextauth_get_action` calls `build_session_probe_response_body(None)`, so `session_status` is `"anonymous"` and `authenticated_principal` is `null` regardless of any `x-account-email` header. The principal-aware branch of that helper exists but is unreachable from this GET handler.
- **Provider validation happens twice, and the second time swallows errors.** The handler first parses the provider with `parse_provider_identifier_as_non_empty` (which *can* return `400`), then the renderer independently re-parses with `NonEmptyText::parse(...).ok()`, silently falling back to the generic `signin_page` body if that second parse fails. The authoritative rejection is the earlier one.
- **A blank provider segment rarely reaches the 400 path.** `split_nextauth_action_into_segments` drops empty segments and `extract_provider_identifier_from_signin_action` filters out empties, so most "empty provider" inputs degrade to a bare `signin` (200, `signin_page`) rather than a `400`. The `400` is a narrow window.
- **Casing and slashes are normalized away.** `/API/Auth/SignIn/Google/` and `signin/google` are equivalent; the classifier only ever sees lowercased, slash-trimmed, whitespace-trimmed segments.
- **`Unrecognized` is total but unreachable via the happy path.** The renderer has an `Unrecognized` arm returning `{"action":"unknown","status":"handled"}`, but `reject_unknown_nextauth_action` returns `404` before rendering — so a client never actually receives the `unknown` envelope. It exists only to keep the pure renderer total.
- **The CSRF token is a fixed placeholder.** `csrf_token` is the literal `"nextauth-csrf-placeholder-token"`; it is not cryptographically issued and must not be trusted as a real anti-CSRF secret.
- **`ApplicationState` is bound but unused** (`_application_state`), and no unit of work is opened — this endpoint is entirely self-contained and cannot fail with a `500`.

#### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Does sending `x-account-email` make `GET /api/auth/session` return my logged-in user?**
A: No. The GET path calls `build_session_probe_response_body(None)` unconditionally. You will always get `session_status: "anonymous"` and `authenticated_principal: null` here, no matter what headers you send.

**Q: Why is `/api/auth/callback/google` a 404 when the providers catalog literally advertises that URL?**
A: Because `callback` is not one of the five recognized leading segments (`csrf`, `providers`, `session`, `signin`, `signout`). The catalog string is a NextAuth-shaped hint, not a route this GET handler services; `classify_nextauth_get_action` returns `Unrecognized` and you get `requested_resource_was_not_found`.

**Q: Can this endpoint ever return a 500?**
A: No. It opens no unit of work, calls no application service, and touches no upstream. There is no `UpstreamApplicationFailure` path in the handler. The only errors it produces are `404` (empty/unknown action) and, narrowly, `400` (a present-but-blank sign-in provider).

---

### `POST /api/auth/*nextauth_action` — NextAuth Catch-All Action Dispatcher (POST)

#### Synopsis

This endpoint is the POST-side of the alma-http NextAuth compatibility shim: a single axum catch-all route (`/api/auth/*nextauth_action`) that fans a mutating NextAuth verb (`signin`, `signout`, `session`, `csrf`, or the `callback/credentials` form) out to one of four internal service branches. The wildcard path segment is normalized, classified into a `NextAuthPostActionKind`, rejected with `404` if unrecognized, and otherwise serviced — with the credentials sign-in branch running a full validation-and-allow-list pipeline against the `allowed_emails` document collection. It returns a JSON envelope describing the outcome of whichever NextAuth concern was requested.

#### Theory & Rationale

NextAuth.js, by architectural fiat, tunnels a menagerie of unrelated authentication concerns — sign-in, sign-out, session refresh, CSRF issuance, provider callbacks — through a single catch-all URL space rooted at `/api/auth/*`. A faithful backend shim therefore cannot express these concerns as separate, semantically-typed routes; it must instead accept the entire wildcard subtree at one handler and recover the client's true intent from the opaque path tail. This handler embraces that constraint rather than fighting it: the `*nextauth_action` wildcard is treated as an untyped command string, normalized into a canonical form, and *then* lifted into a strongly-typed `NextAuthPostActionKind` enum so that all subsequent branching happens over a closed, exhaustive set of intents rather than over stringly-typed spaghetti. This is the classic "parse, don't validate" discipline applied at the routing boundary.

On REST semantics: this is a `POST`, and deliberately so. Every action reachable here is non-safe and non-idempotent in principle — a credentials sign-in mints session state, a sign-out tears it down, a CSRF issuance produces a fresh token. `POST` is the correct verb precisely because none of these operations promise that repeating the request leaves the server in the same state, and none may be cached or prefetched. In Domain-Driven Design terms the handler is a thin *application-layer* orchestrator sitting in the `auth` bounded context: it owns no domain invariants of its own, delegates email validity to the `Email` value object, delegates callback-URL non-emptiness to the `NonEmptyText` value object, and delegates the allow-list decision to the `DocumentCollectionPort`. The handler's only real responsibility is translation — from HTTP wire concerns into domain vocabulary and back — which is exactly where an application service belongs.

#### Authentication & Required Headers

| Header | Required | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x-request-id` | No (recommended) | `x-request-id: 6f1c2d9a-3b4e-4c8a-9f10-2a7b6c5d4e3f` | Correlation identifier echoed through logs/traces for this request. Not read by this handler's body, but honored by the surrounding middleware stack for observability. Supply a UUID per request so failures in the credentials pipeline can be traced end to end. |
| `x-account-email` | No (for this endpoint) | `x-account-email: user@example.com` | The ambient caller-identity header used by authenticated endpoints elsewhere in alma-http. This particular handler does **not** read `x-account-email`; the email that drives the allow-list check comes from the request *body* (`email` field), not this header. Present here for consistency with the rest of the API surface. |

**The type-state pipeline (Validated → Authenticated → Authorized).** Although this handler does not consume a request-guard extractor for identity, the credentials sign-in branch reproduces the same three-phase progression in ordinary code, and understanding it is essential to reading the error table below:

- **Validated** — the raw submitted body is coerced into a shape the domain will accept. `deserialize_credentials_from_submitted_body` insists the body be a JSON object; `extract_email_field_from_credentials_payload` insists an `email` field is present; `extract_csrf_token_field_from_body` insists a `csrfToken` field is present. Failures here are *shape* failures and surface as `400 RequestBodyWasMalformed`.
- **Authenticated** — the validated material is proven to be genuine credential material. `parse_submitted_email_as_value_object` proves the email is a well-formed `Email` (a malformed email during sign-in is treated as a credential fault, not a generic bad request), and `validate_submitted_csrf_token_shape` proves the CSRF token is long enough and free of illegal characters. Failures here surface as `401 AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`.
- **Authorized** — the now-authenticated email is checked against policy. `verify_submitted_email_is_allowed` consults the `allowed_emails` collection and `reject_when_email_is_not_allowed` gates the flow. A caller with perfectly valid, well-formed credentials who is simply not on the allow list is *authenticated but not authorized*, and surfaces as `403 AuthorizationWasDenied`.

Each phase strictly precedes the next; you can never be authorized without first being authenticated, and never authenticated without first being validated.

#### Path & Query Parameters

| Name | In | Type | Required | Constraints | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `nextauth_action` | path (wildcard) | `String` | Yes | Captured by the axum `*nextauth_action` catch-all; may contain multiple slash-separated segments. After normalization must classify to one of `signin` / `signin/credentials` / `callback/credentials` / `signout` / `session` / `csrf`, else `404`. | None | The NextAuth verb (and optional sub-path) that selects which action branch runs. Leading/trailing slashes, surrounding whitespace, a trailing `?query`, and letter case are all stripped/normalized before classification. |

No query parameters are read by this handler. Any query string present on the URL is discarded during path normalization (`normalize_nextauth_action_path_segment` splits on `?` and keeps only the segment before it).

#### Request Body

The credentials sign-in branch is *designed* to read the following fields from a JSON object body. **Important:** in the current handler wiring, `handle_nextauth_action_via_post` extracts only `State` and `Path` and does **not** attach an axum `Json`/body extractor, so at runtime the credentials branch is serviced against a hard-coded empty object (`Value::Object(serde_json::Map::new())`). The field contract below therefore describes what the validation helpers enforce (and what they are unit-tested against directly), which is also what a future wiring that adds a body extractor would consume. Fields are read from the JSON object; string fields are trimmed and empty strings are treated as absent.

(a) **Field table**

| Field | Type | Required | Constraints | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `email` | `string` | Yes (credentials branch) | Trimmed; must be non-empty; must parse as a valid domain `Email`. Missing → `400`. Malformed → `401`. | None | The sign-in email. Drives the case-insensitive allow-list lookup key. |
| `csrfToken` | `string` | Yes (credentials branch) | Trimmed; must be non-empty; after trimming must be ≥ 16 characters and contain no whitespace or control characters. Missing/empty → `400`. Too short / illegal chars → `401`. | None | The NextAuth CSRF token; shape-validated, not cryptographically verified here. |
| `callbackUrl` | `string` | No | Trimmed; if present must be non-empty (must parse as `NonEmptyText`); empty/whitespace-only after presence → `400`. | `null` | Optional post-sign-in redirect target, echoed back in the success body as `callback_url`. |

(b) **JSON Schema (draft 2020-12)**

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "https://alma.example/schemas/nextauth-post-credentials-body.json",
  "title": "SubmittedCredentialsPayload",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "email": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1,
      "description": "Sign-in email; must parse as a valid domain Email after trimming."
    },
    "csrfToken": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 16,
      "description": "NextAuth CSRF token; must be >= 16 chars with no whitespace/control characters after trimming."
    },
    "callbackUrl": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1,
      "description": "Optional post-sign-in redirect target."
    }
  },
  "required": ["email", "csrfToken"],
  "additionalProperties": true
}
```

(c) **TypeScript interface**

```typescript
/**
 * Body the credentials sign-in branch is designed to read.
 * NextAuth submits "JSON-with-anything", so unrelated keys are ignored
 * (additionalProperties: true).
 */
interface SubmittedCredentialsBody {
  /** Required. Sign-in email; must parse as a valid domain Email. */
  email: string;
  /** Required. CSRF token; >= 16 chars, no whitespace/control chars. */
  csrfToken: string;
  /** Optional. Post-sign-in redirect target; echoed as `callback_url`. */
  callbackUrl?: string;
}
```

(d) **Rust struct mirror**

```rust
/// Loosely typed view over the credentials NextAuth submits for a sign in
/// attempt. The real body is JSON-with-anything, so extracted fields stay
/// optional and are validated in dedicated helpers.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct SubmittedCredentialsPayload {
    pub email_field: Option<String>,
    pub csrf_token_field: Option<String>,
    pub callback_url_field: Option<String>,
}
```

#### Request Examples

The `signin` action is shown with a credentials body (the shape the pipeline validates). Note the runtime caveat above regarding the empty-object body.

```bash
# curl — credentials sign-in
curl -X POST 'https://api.alma.example/api/auth/signin' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'x-request-id: 6f1c2d9a-3b4e-4c8a-9f10-2a7b6c5d4e3f' \
  -H 'x-account-email: user@example.com' \
  -d '{
    "email": "user@example.com",
    "csrfToken": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef",
    "callbackUrl": "/dashboard"
  }'
```

```bash
# HTTPie — csrf token issuance (no body needed)
http POST 'https://api.alma.example/api/auth/csrf' \
  x-request-id:6f1c2d9a-3b4e-4c8a-9f10-2a7b6c5d4e3f \
  x-account-email:user@example.com
```

```javascript
// fetch — credentials sign-in
const response = await fetch("https://api.alma.example/api/auth/signin", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "x-request-id": "6f1c2d9a-3b4e-4c8a-9f10-2a7b6c5d4e3f",
    "x-account-email": "user@example.com",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    email: "user@example.com",
    csrfToken: "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef",
    callbackUrl: "/dashboard",
  }),
});
const payload = await response.json();
console.log(payload.status); // "signed_in" on success
```

#### Successful Response

Status `200 OK`, `Content-Type: application/json`. The exact shape depends on the action branch. All four success shapes are documented; only the credentials branch has nested structure.

**Response field table**

| Field | Type | Branch | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `status` | `string` | all | Outcome tag: `signed_in`, `signed_out`, `session_refreshed`, or `csrf_issued`. |
| `provider` | `string` | credentials | Always `"credentials"` on the sign-in branch. |
| `user` | `object` | credentials | Object holding the authenticated identity. |
| `user.email` | `string` | credentials | The validated, allow-listed email that signed in. |
| `callback_url` | `string \| null` | credentials | Echoed redirect target, or `null` when no `callbackUrl` was supplied. |
| `action` | `string` | signout / session / csrf | The normalized action string that was serviced. |

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "https://alma.example/schemas/nextauth-post-signin-success.json",
  "title": "SignInSuccessBody",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "status": { "type": "string", "const": "signed_in" },
    "provider": { "type": "string", "const": "credentials" },
    "user": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": { "email": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 } },
      "required": ["email"],
      "additionalProperties": false
    },
```
