**Realistic 200 example (credentials sign-in)**

```json
{
  "status": "signed_in",
  "provider": "credentials",
  "user": {
    "email": "user@example.com"
  },
  "callback_url": "/dashboard"
}
```

#### Error Responses

Every `HttpError` variant that this endpoint can produce, plus the standard variants of the shared error enum. `error_category` is the serialized category tag on the shared `SerializedErrorBody`.

| Status | error_category | When (for THIS endpoint) | Example body |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400 | `RequestBodyWasMalformed` | Credentials body is not a JSON object; `email` field missing; `csrfToken` field missing/empty; a present `callbackUrl` is empty/whitespace-only. | `{"error_category":"RequestBodyWasMalformed","error_explanation":"credentials body is missing an 'email' field"}` |
| 401 | `AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing` | Not raised directly by this handler; reserved by the shared error enum for absent credentials on guarded routes. | `{"error_category":"AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing","error_explanation":"authentication credentials were missing"}` |
| 401 | `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid` | Submitted `email` fails to parse as a domain `Email`; CSRF token shorter than 16 chars after trimming; CSRF token contains whitespace or control characters. | `{"error_category":"AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid","error_explanation":"submitted CSRF token is too short to be valid"}` |
| 403 | `AuthorizationWasDenied` | The submitted email is well-formed but is not present in the `allowed_emails` collection (neither direct-key match nor full-scan match). | `{"error_category":"AuthorizationWasDenied","error_explanation":"email 'user@example.com' is not on the sign-in allow list"}` |
| 404 | `RequestedResourceWasNotFound` | The normalized wildcard action classifies to `Unknown` (e.g. `providers`, `verify-request`, any unrecognized verb). | `{"error_category":"RequestedResourceWasNotFound","error_explanation":"no NextAuth POST action is registered for 'providers'"}` |
| 500 | `UpstreamApplicationFailure` | The `DocumentCollectionPort` fails while fetching or listing `allowed_emails` documents during the allow-list check (propagated via `?`). | `{"error_category":"UpstreamApplicationFailure","error_explanation":"document collection backend unavailable"}` |

**Full `SerializedErrorBody` example**

```json
{
  "error_category": "AuthorizationWasDenied",
  "error_explanation": "email 'user@example.com' is not on the sign-in allow list"
}
```

#### Internal Processing Pipeline

The real helper functions invoked, in call order for the credentials branch (the other three branches short-circuit at step 3 with a static JSON body):

1. `normalize_nextauth_action_path_segment(raw_action)` — strips a query string, trims whitespace, strips leading/trailing slashes, and lowercases the wildcard segment into a canonical form.
2. `classify_nextauth_post_action(&normalized_action)` — maps the normalized string onto a `NextAuthPostActionKind` (`CredentialsSignIn`, `SignOut`, `Session`, `CsrfToken`, or `Unknown`).
3. `reject_unknown_nextauth_post_action(&action_kind, &normalized_action)` — converts an `Unknown` classification into `404 RequestedResourceWasNotFound`; known actions pass through.
4. `service_credentials_signin(&document_collection, &submitted_body)` — orchestrates the whole credentials flow (steps 5–13 below).
5. `deserialize_credentials_from_submitted_body(&submitted_body)` — validates the body is a JSON object and extracts trimmed, non-empty `email`/`csrfToken`/`callbackUrl` fields into `SubmittedCredentialsPayload`.
6. `extract_email_field_from_credentials_payload(&credentials_payload)` — pulls the `email` out, or `400` if absent.
7. `parse_submitted_email_as_value_object(email_candidate)` — parses the email into the domain `Email` value object, mapping domain failure to `401` invalid credentials via `map_credentials_domain_error_to_invalid_credentials`.
8. `extract_csrf_token_field_from_body(&submitted_body)` — pulls the `csrfToken`, or `400` if missing/empty.
9. `validate_submitted_csrf_token_shape(&csrf_token)` — enforces min-length 16 and rejects whitespace/control characters (`401` on failure).
10. `extract_callback_url_field_from_body(&submitted_body)` — optionally reads `callbackUrl`, returning `None` when absent.
11. `parse_callback_url_as_non_empty(candidate)` — parses a present callback URL into `NonEmptyText`, mapping emptiness to `400`.
12. `verify_submitted_email_is_allowed(&document_collection, &authenticated_email)` — builds the lowercase lookup key (`build_allowed_emails_collection_lookup_key`), does a direct `fetch_document` on `allowed_emails`, then falls back to a full `list_documents` scan comparing normalized bodies/identifiers.
13. `reject_when_email_is_not_allowed(email_is_allowed, &authenticated_email)` — converts a `false` allow-list decision into `403 AuthorizationWasDenied`.
14. `build_signin_success_response_body(&authenticated_email, callback_url.as_ref())` — assembles the `signed_in` JSON envelope, embedding the callback URL or `null`.

#### Edge Cases & Gotchas

- **The runtime body is always empty.** `handle_nextauth_action_via_post` extracts only `State` and `Path`; it never attaches a `Json`/body extractor. The credentials branch is serviced against `Value::Object(serde_json::Map::new())`, so *as currently wired* the sign-in flow reaches step 6 and fails with `400 "credentials body is missing an 'email' field"` regardless of what body the client actually sent. The validation helpers are correct and unit-tested directly; only the wiring omits the extractor.
- **The three non-credentials branches ignore the body entirely and always succeed with a static envelope.** `signout`, `session`, and `csrf` never touch the allow-list store and cannot return `401`/`403`/`500`; they return `200` with `status` and `action` fields and nothing else. There is no real sign-out or CSRF minting happening — these are stub envelopes.
- **Query strings on the path are silently discarded.** `normalize_nextauth_action_path_segment` splits on `?` and keeps only the left side, so `/api/auth/csrf?callbackUrl=/x` is classified exactly as `csrf`. Anything you wanted from the query string is lost.
- **Action matching is case- and slash-insensitive but otherwise strict.** `/SignIn/Credentials/` normalizes to `signin/credentials` and is accepted; but `signin/email` or `providers` classify to `Unknown` and yield `404`. Only the five exact normalized forms are recognized.
- **The allow-list check has an O(n) fallback scan.** If the direct-key `fetch_document` misses, the handler lists *every* document in `allowed_emails` and compares normalized bodies and identifiers. On a large allow-list this is a full-collection read per sign-in attempt, and a backend failure at either the fetch or the list stage propagates as `500 UpstreamApplicationFailure`.
- **A malformed email is a `401`, not a `400`.** Deliberately: during sign-in a bad email is treated as invalid *credential material* rather than a generic malformed body, so it maps through `map_credentials_domain_error_to_invalid_credentials` to `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`.
- **CSRF token validation is shape-only.** The token is checked for length (≥16) and legal characters, never verified against a stored/issued token. A 16+ character garbage string with no whitespace passes step 9.
- **Allow-list keys are case-insensitive.** `build_allowed_emails_collection_lookup_key` lowercases and trims, so `User@Example.COM` and `user@example.com` collide to the same key.

#### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: I sent a perfectly valid `email` and `csrfToken` in the body and still got `400 "missing an 'email' field"`. Is my JSON wrong?**
A: Your JSON is probably fine. The handler does not read the body at all in its current wiring — it validates against a hard-coded empty object. Until a `Json` extractor is added to the handler signature, the credentials branch cannot see your body. This is a wiring gap, not a client error.

**Q: Does the `session` POST action actually refresh my session?**
A: No. It returns `{"status":"session_refreshed","action":"session"}` and touches no session store. It is a static stub. The same is true of `signout` and `csrf`.

**Q: Why is a bad email a `401` and a missing email a `400`? Aren't they both "bad body"?**
A: Structurally, yes; semantically, no. A missing field is a shape problem (`400 RequestBodyWasMalformed`), whereas a syntactically-present-but-invalid email is treated as bad credential material during authentication (`401 AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`). The distinction mirrors the Validated → Authenticated phase boundary.

**Q: The path is a wildcard — can I invent my own action like `/api/auth/magic-link`?**
A: You can request it; you will receive `404 RequestedResourceWasNotFound` with `"no NextAuth POST action is registered for 'magic-link'"`. Only `signin`, `signin/credentials`, `callback/credentials`, `signout`, `session`, and `csrf` (post-normalization) are serviced.

### `GET /api/allowed-emails` — List the Application Access Allow-List

#### Synopsis

Returns the set of email addresses that are permitted to access the application, drawn from the persisted `allowed_emails` document collection. The persisted allow-list is deliberately augmented with the currently authenticated principal so that the caller *always* appears in the response, even when it has not yet been explicitly recorded in the collection. The response is a JSON object carrying a deterministically sorted, case-insensitively de-duplicated array of email strings alongside a convenience `total_count`.

#### Theory & Rationale

This endpoint is a textbook exercise in REST read semantics. It is a `GET`, and it is therefore both **safe** (it mutates no server-observable state) and **idempotent** (issuing it once or one thousand times leaves the persisted allow-list exactly as it was found). The one subtlety worth noting is that the response is *not* a verbatim transcription of the underlying collection: the handler synthesizes an augmented view by folding the requesting principal into the returned set. This is a *representational* transformation, not a *state* transformation — the collection on disk is never written to — so safety and idempotency are preserved in the strict HTTP sense even though two different callers will observe two subtly different bodies. Because the augmentation is a pure function of the request's authenticated identity, the endpoint remains referentially transparent per-principal: the same principal against the same collection state always yields the same body.

In Domain-Driven Design terms, this handler lives squarely in the HTTP delivery layer and is a thin orchestration seam over the `DocumentCollectionPort` application port. It performs no domain reasoning beyond validating raw strings into `Email` value objects; the `Email` value object itself is the domain's guardian of the "what is a well-formed address" invariant, and this handler simply defers to `Email::parse` at every boundary. The allow-list is modeled as an anemic collection of documents rather than a rich aggregate precisely because access-control membership here is a flat set with no lifecycle, no invariants beyond per-element well-formedness, and no transactional consistency requirements — the very definition of a place where a document collection port, rather than a repository over an aggregate root, is the correct DDD placement.

#### Authentication & Required Headers

Every request is funneled through the `HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>` extractor before the handler body ever runs. That extractor reads exactly two headers.

| Header | Required | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x-account-email` | **Yes** | `x-account-email: person@example.com` | The authenticated principal. Absent → `401 authentication_credentials_were_missing`. Present but not valid UTF-8 text, or present but not parseable as an email, → `401 authentication_credentials_were_invalid`. |
| `x-request-id` | No (optional) | `x-request-id: 7f3a9c2e-1b4d-4e8a-9f01-abcdef012345` | Correlation identifier for tracing. If absent, the pipeline substitutes the literal string `unassigned-correlation-identifier`. Note: if the header *is* supplied but is empty/whitespace, the `validate()` stage rejects it with `400 request_body_was_malformed`. |

**The type-state pipeline (`Validated -> Authenticated -> Authorized`).** Authentication and authorization are enforced at compile time via a phantom-typed state machine, `HttpRequestInPipeline<PipelineStage>`. The handler's signature demands `HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>`; it is *impossible* for the handler body to execute unless the extractor has walked the request all the way to the terminal `RequestHasBeenAuthorized` state. Concretely, inside `from_request_parts` the extractor:

1. Resolves the correlation identifier from `x-request-id` (falling back to `unassigned-correlation-identifier`).
2. Reads `x-account-email`; a missing header short-circuits to `AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing`, and a non-textual header short-circuits to `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`.
3. Runs the raw header value through `email_string_prism().preview(...)`; failure short-circuits to `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`.
4. Calls `HttpRequestInPipeline::originate(correlation_identifier).validate()?` — producing `RequestHasBeenValidated` (rejects an empty correlation identifier with `RequestBodyWasMalformed`).
5. Calls `.authenticate(parsed_authenticated_principal)?` — producing `RequestHasBeenAuthenticated` and stashing the principal in `declared_principal`.
6. Calls `.authorize()?` — producing `RequestHasBeenAuthorized`; if no principal is present this yields `AuthorizationWasDenied` (unreachable on this path because authentication always sets the principal, but the type forces the check).

Only the value returned by step 6 satisfies the handler's parameter type. There is no way to forge, skip, or reorder these stages: `validate`, `authenticate`, and `authorize` are each defined on exactly one input state and each return exactly one output state, so the compiler mechanically enforces `Validated -> Authenticated -> Authorized`.

#### Path & Query Parameters

None. This endpoint takes no path segments and reads no query-string parameters whatsoever. Any query string appended to the URL is accepted by the router and silently ignored by the handler.

#### Request Body

This endpoint reads **no request body**. It is a `GET` handler whose only inputs are HTTP headers (consumed by the extractor) and the persisted collection state; the handler function signature contains no body extractor (no `Json<...>`, no `Bytes`, no form). Any body sent with the request is ignored.

For completeness, the accepted request body is the empty object.

(a) Field table — there are no body fields to document.

| Field | Type | Required | Constraints | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| *(none)* | — | — | — | — | This endpoint reads no request body. |

(b) JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for the (empty) request body:

```json

  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "ListAllowedEmailsRequestBody",
  "description": "GET /api/allowed-emails reads no request body.",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {},
  "additionalProperties": false
}
```

#### Request Examples


```javascript
// fetch
const response = await fetch("https://api.alma.example.com/api/allowed-emails", {
  method: "GET",
  headers: {
    "x-account-email": "person@example.com",
    "x-request-id": "7f3a9c2e-1b4d-4e8a-9f01-abcdef012345",

});

if (!response.ok) {
  const errorBody = await response.json(); // { error_category, error_explanation }
  throw new Error(`${response.status} ${errorBody.error_category}: ${errorBody.error_explanation}`);
}

const { allowed_emails, total_count } = await response.json();
console.log(`${total_count} allowed emails:`, allowed_emails);
```

#### Successful Response

**Status:** `200 OK`, `Content-Type: application/json`.

Response field table:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `allowed_emails` | `string[]` | The augmented, de-duplicated (case-insensitive), alphabetically-sorted (case-insensitive) list of permitted email addresses. Each element is a validated, normalized email string. Always includes the requesting principal. May be empty only if the collection is empty *and* the requesting principal somehow fails to append — in practice the caller's own email is always present, so the array is non-empty for any successful request. |
| `total_count` | `integer` (unsigned) | The number of elements in `allowed_emails`. Exactly `allowed_emails.length`; provided as a convenience so callers need not compute it. |

```json
    "alice@example.com",
```

#### Error Responses

Every error is serialized by `HttpError::into_response` as a JSON object of shape `{ "error_category": string, "error_explanation": string }` with the corresponding status code.

| Status | error_category | When (for THIS endpoint) | Example body |
|---|---|---|---|
| `400` | `request_body_was_malformed` | Only reachable via the pipeline's `validate()` stage — an empty/whitespace `x-request-id` correlation identifier. This endpoint has no request body of its own to malform. | `{"error_category":"request_body_was_malformed","error_explanation":"the correlation identifier was empty"}` |
| `401` | `authentication_credentials_were_missing` | The `x-account-email` header is absent entirely. | `{"error_category":"authentication_credentials_were_missing","error_explanation":"the 'x-account-email' header was absent"}` |
| `401` | `authentication_credentials_were_invalid` | The `x-account-email` header is present but not valid text, or does not parse as an email (extractor), or the authorized principal fails a second `Email::parse` inside the handler (`parse_requesting_account_as_email`). | `{"error_category":"authentication_credentials_were_invalid","error_explanation":"the account header did not parse into a valid email address"}` |
| `403` | `authorization_was_denied` | The document-collection port returns `ApplicationError::AuthorizationWasDenied` while listing (mapped by `map_document_collection_failure_to_http_error`). Also the pipeline's `authorize()` guard, though that is unreachable on the authenticated path. | `{"error_category":"authorization_was_denied","error_explanation":"authorization was denied"}` |
| `404` | `requested_resource_was_not_found` | The port returns `RequestedResourceCouldNotBeLocated` or `RequestedProjectCouldNotBeLocated` for the `allowed_emails` collection (e.g. the collection does not exist in the backing store). | `{"error_category":"requested_resource_was_not_found","error_explanation":"the requested resource could not be located"}` |
| `500` | `upstream_application_failure` | Any other `ApplicationError` from `list_documents` (connectivity, serialization, backing-store failure, etc.). | `{"error_category":"upstream_application_failure","error_explanation":"document collection failure: boom"}` |

Full `SerializedErrorBody` example (a `404` here):

```json
{
  "error_category": "requested_resource_was_not_found",
  "error_explanation": "the requested resource could not be located"
}
```

#### Internal Processing Pipeline

The handler is decomposed into a long chain of single-purpose helpers; in call order:

1. `extract_requesting_account_principal(&authorized_request)` — pulls the raw authenticated principal string out of the `RequestHasBeenAuthorized` pipeline stage via `authorized_principal().as_str()`.
2. `parse_requesting_account_as_email(principal)` — re-validates that principal string as an `Email`; a failure surfaces as `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid` (a malformed principal implies a broken auth pipeline, not a bad body).
3. `allowed_emails_collection_name()` — returns the `&'static str` constant `ALLOWED_EMAILS_COLLECTION_NAME` (`"allowed_emails"`).
4. `load_allowed_email_documents(&application_state.document_collection, collection_name)` — calls `DocumentCollectionPort::list_documents(...)` and maps any port failure via helper (15).
5. `collect_valid_allowed_emails_from_documents(stored_documents)` — filter-maps documents into validated `Email`s, internally calling (6) and (7) below and silently dropping unusable entries.
6. `extract_email_string_from_stored_document(&doc)` — reads a candidate email from a bare-string body, or from an object body's `email` field (falling back to `email_address`); anything else yields `None`.
7. `parse_stored_email_string_as_value_object(candidate)` — `Email::parse(...).ok()`, discarding entries that fail validation rather than aborting.
8. `append_requesting_account_when_absent(&mut allowed_emails, requesting_account_email)` — appends the caller's email unless a case-insensitive match already exists.
9. `deduplicate_allowed_emails_preserving_order(allowed_emails)` — removes case-insensitive duplicates, keeping the first occurrence in place.
10. `sort_allowed_emails_case_insensitively(&mut allowed_emails)` — sorts by ASCII-lowercased address for a deterministic order.
11. `count_total_allowed_emails(&allowed_emails)` — returns the `.len()` used for `total_count`.
12. `serialize_allowed_emails_collection(&allowed_emails)` — maps each `Email` to a JSON string via (13) `serialize_allowed_email_to_json_value`.
13. `build_allowed_emails_response_body(serialized_emails, total_count)` — assembles the final `{ "allowed_emails": [...], "total_count": n }` JSON object.
14. `map_document_collection_failure_to_http_error(port_failure)` — (helper 15 in source order) translates `ApplicationError` into `404` / `403` / `500` `HttpError` variants.
15. `emails_match_case_insensitively(a, b)` — the case-insensitive comparison primitive used by helpers 8 and 9.

#### Edge Cases & Gotchas

- **The caller is always in the list.** Even if `allowed_emails` is entirely empty (or missing the caller), `append_requesting_account_when_absent` guarantees the requesting principal appears in the response. A `200` response therefore always contains at least one element for an authenticated caller.
- **Two `Email::parse` passes on the principal.** The extractor already parses `x-account-email` into an `Email`, yet the handler re-parses the same principal via `parse_requesting_account_as_email`. On the normal path this is redundant, but a failure there is reported as `401 authentication_credentials_were_invalid`, *not* `400`.
- **Malformed stored entries are silently dropped, not errored.** A document whose body is neither a bare string nor an object with `email`/`email_address`, or whose email fails validation, is quietly filtered out by `collect_valid_allowed_emails_from_documents`. You will never get a `500` because one row in the collection is garbage — it just vanishes from the output.
- **Case-insensitivity everywhere, and `Email::parse` normalizes casing.** De-duplication, the caller-presence check, and sorting are all case-insensitive; additionally `Email::parse` lowercases addresses, so `Alice@X.com` is stored/returned as `alice@x.com`. Do not rely on the original casing of stored addresses surviving.
- **`email` wins over `email_address`.** For object-bodied documents, the `email` field is preferred; `email_address` is only consulted when `email` is absent. A document carrying both returns the `email` value.
- **Empty `x-request-id` is a `400`, missing `x-request-id` is fine.** Omitting the header entirely yields the fallback `unassigned-correlation-identifier` and succeeds; sending it as an empty/whitespace string trips `validate()` and returns `400 request_body_was_malformed`.
- **`403`/`404` originate from the store, not from access rules on the endpoint itself.** This endpoint does not do per-resource authorization of the allow-list beyond the pipeline; a `403`/`404` here reflects what `list_documents` reported for the `allowed_emails` collection.

#### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Can I filter, paginate, or search the allow-list via query parameters?**
A: No. The handler reads zero query parameters. It returns the entire (augmented, de-duplicated, sorted) list every time. Filter client-side.

**Q: If I hit this endpoint, does my email get added to the persisted allow-list?**
A: No. The augmentation is representational only — your email is folded into the *response* body, never written back. The `GET` is safe and idempotent; the backing collection is untouched.

**Q: I sent a JSON body / a wrong `Content-Type`. Why did nothing change?**
A: Because there is no body extractor on this handler. Bodies are ignored outright. The only things that matter are the `x-account-email` and (optionally) `x-request-id` headers.

### `GET /api/debug-oauth-scopes` — Report the OAuth Scopes Granted to the Authenticated Principal

#### Synopsis

This endpoint reports, in exhaustive descriptor form, the set of OAuth scopes that the currently authenticated principal would be granted by this service. The report is derived entirely from static, in-process configuration — there is no per-account scope customisation, no database access, and no upstream call — so the handler merely validates the caller, assembles the descriptor collection, and serialises it. An optional scope filter, placed in through the pipeline's correlation identifier (there being no request body or query extractor), narrows the returned set to the intersection of requested-and-granted scopes.

#### Theory & Rationale

Within the taxonomy of REST verbs this is the archetypal safe, idempotent, side-effect-free `GET`: it is a pure projection of server-side state onto a JSON representation, and calling it once, twice, or ten thousand times leaves the world exactly as it found it. Because the resource being read ("the scopes I would be granted") is a *computed* view rather than a stored aggregate, the handler performs zero persistence access; it is a read model in the purest CQRS sense, materialised on demand from configuration constants (`default_granted_oauth_scope_identifiers` and `optional_offline_access_scope_identifiers`) rather than reconstituted from an event stream or a row in a table. This makes the endpoint trivially cacheable in principle and eminently well-behaved under retry, since the safety guarantee of `GET` is not merely conventional here but structurally enforced by the total absence of a `UnitOfWork` interaction (the `State<ApplicationState<..>>` extractor is bound to `_application_state` and deliberately ignored).

From a Domain-Driven Design standpoint the handler sits squarely in the `auth` bounded context and consumes the domain's ubiquitous value objects — `Email` for the principal and `NonEmptyText` for the raw scope filter — rather than passing naked strings around. Validation is pushed to the boundary: the principal string extracted from the type-state pipeline is re-parsed through `Email::parse`, and the optional filter is coerced through `NonEmptyText::parse`, so that malformed input is rejected (or, for the debug filter specifically, silently downgraded to "no filter") before any business logic runs. The endpoint's naming (`debug-oauth-scopes`) and its placement outside the canonical `/api/auth/*` sub-tree telegraph its diagnostic intent: it is an introspection facility, not a scope-provisioning command, and it therefore deliberately owns no write capability whatsoever.

#### Authentication & Required Headers

| Header | Required | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x-account-email` | **Yes** | `x-account-email: scientist@example.com` | The authenticated principal. If absent → `401 AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing`. If present but not valid UTF-8 text, or not parseable as an email → `401 AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`. Re-validated a second time inside the handler via `Email::parse`. |
| `x-request-id` | No (recommended) | `x-request-id: 7b9f...;scopes=openid email` | The correlation identifier. If absent it defaults to the literal `"unassigned-correlation-identifier"`. It doubles as the *only* caller-influenced channel for the optional scope filter: a `scopes=` fragment (see below) embedded here is honoured as a filter. |

**The type-state pipeline (`Validated → Authenticated → Authorized`).** This endpoint does not receive raw `axum` request parts; it receives a `HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>`, a value whose *type parameter* proves, at compile time, that the request has traversed the full authentication ladder. The ladder is walked inside the `FromRequestParts` extractor before the handler body ever runs:

1. **Originate → Validated.** The `x-request-id` header is read (defaulting to `"unassigned-correlation-identifier"` when missing). `HttpRequestInPipeline::originate(..).validate()` rejects an *empty/blank* correlation identifier with `400 RequestBodyWasMalformed`; because a default is always substituted, this branch is effectively unreachable for real traffic.
2. **Validated → Authenticated.** The `x-account-email` header is read. Absence yields `401 AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing`; a non-text value yields `401 AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`; a value that fails the `email_string_prism` yields `401 AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`. On success `.authenticate(principal)` attaches the parsed `Email`.
3. **Authenticated → Authorized.** `.authorize()` confirms a principal is present (it always is at this point) and produces the `RequestHasBeenAuthorized` witness; a missing principal here would produce `403 AuthorizationWasDenied`. Only this final type exposes `authorized_principal()` and `correlation_identifier()`, so the handler is *statically incapable* of reading an unauthenticated principal.

#### Path & Query Parameters

None. This endpoint declares no path segments beyond the literal `/api/debug-oauth-scopes` and consumes no `axum` `Query` extractor. The optional scope filter is *not* a query parameter — it is parsed out of the `x-request-id` header value (see Request Body and Edge Cases).

#### Request Body

This endpoint reads **no request body**. It is a `GET` with no `Json<..>` or other body extractor in its signature; any bytes sent in the body are ignored entirely.

The only caller-supplied, request-scoped datum the handler interprets is the optional scope filter, which is *not* a body field but a `scopes=` fragment carried inside the `x-request-id` correlation header. For completeness it is described here as if it were a field.

(a) Pseudo-field table (parsed from the `x-request-id` header, not from a body):

| Field | Type | Required | Constraints | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `scopes` (fragment) | string | No | Extracted from the first `;`-separated segment of `x-request-id` beginning with `scopes=`. Tokens split on space and comma; empty tokens dropped. Every token must be a *recognized* scope (`openid`, `email`, `profile`, `offline_access`) or the request fails with `400 RequestBodyWasMalformed`. A non-blank value that fails `NonEmptyText::parse` is silently treated as "no filter". | absent → no filter (full granted set returned) | Narrows the report to the intersection of the requested scopes and the granted scopes, preserving granted-set order. |

(b) JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) — the request body itself is empty:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "ListOAuthScopesRequestBody",
  "type": "object",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {},
  "description": "This endpoint accepts no request body. The optional 'scopes=' filter is carried in the x-request-id header, not here."
}
```

(c) TypeScript interface:

```typescript
// GET /api/debug-oauth-scopes accepts no request body.
// The optional scope filter travels in the `x-request-id` header, e.g.
//   "x-request-id": "corr-123;scopes=openid email"
export type ListOAuthScopesRequestBody = Record<string, never>;
```

(d) Rust struct mirror (illustrative — the handler binds no body extractor):

```rust

/// The scope filter is recovered from the correlation identifier, not deserialized.
#[derive(Debug, Default, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct ListOAuthScopesRequestBody {}
```

#### Request Examples

curl (no filter):

```bash
  -H 'x-account-email: scientist@example.com' \
  -H 'x-request-id: 7b9f2c1a-corr-0001'
```

curl (with a `scopes=` filter placed in the correlation header):

```bash
curl -sS -X GET 'https://api.alma.example.com/api/debug-oauth-scopes' \
  -H 'x-account-email: scientist@example.com' \
  -H 'x-request-id: 7b9f2c1a-corr-0001;scopes=openid email'
```

HTTPie:

```bash
http GET 'https://api.alma.example.com/api/debug-oauth-scopes' \
  x-account-email:scientist@example.com \
  x-request-id:'7b9f2c1a-corr-0001;scopes=openid,email,offline_access'
```

JavaScript `fetch`:

```javascript
const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.alma.example.com/api/debug-oauth-scopes",
  {
    method: "GET",
    headers: {
      "x-account-email": "scientist@example.com",
      // Append ";scopes=..." to filter; omit to receive the full granted set.
      "x-request-id": "7b9f2c1a-corr-0001;scopes=openid email profile",
    },
  }
);
const report = await response.json();
console.log(report.scope_count, report.includes_offline_access);
```

#### Successful Response

`200 OK` with a JSON object assembled by `build_oauth_scopes_report_body`.

Response field table:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `oauth_scopes` | array of objects | One descriptor per effective scope, in granted-set order (`openid`, `email`, `profile`, `offline_access`). |
| `oauth_scopes[].identifier` | string | The scope identifier, e.g. `"openid"`. |
| `oauth_scopes[].label` | string | Human-readable label: `OpenID sign-in`, `Email address`, `Basic profile`, `Offline access (refresh token)`, or `Unknown scope`. |
| `oauth_scopes[].grants_offline_access` | boolean | `true` only for the `offline_access` identifier. |
| `scope_count` | integer | Count of entries in `oauth_scopes` (`serialized_scopes.len()`). |
| `includes_offline_access` | boolean | `true` if the effective set contains `offline_access`. |

Response JSON Schema (draft 2020-12):

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "OAuthScopesReport",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["oauth_scopes", "scope_count", "includes_offline_access"],
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "oauth_scopes": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "required": ["identifier", "label", "grants_offline_access"],
        "additionalProperties": false,
        "properties": {
          "identifier": { "type": "string" },
          "label": { "type": "string" },
          "grants_offline_access": { "type": "boolean" }
        }
      }
    },
    "scope_count": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0 },
    "includes_offline_access": { "type": "boolean" }
  }
}
```

Realistic `200` example (no filter — full granted set):

```json
{
  "oauth_scopes": [
    { "identifier": "openid", "label": "OpenID sign-in", "grants_offline_access": false },
    { "identifier": "email", "label": "Email address", "grants_offline_access": false },
    { "identifier": "profile", "label": "Basic profile", "grants_offline_access": false },
    { "identifier": "offline_access", "label": "Offline access (refresh token)", "grants_offline_access": true }
  ],
  "scope_count": 4,
  "includes_offline_access": true
}
```

#### Error Responses

Every `HttpError` variant is serialised through `SerializedErrorBody` as `{ error_category, error_explanation }`. The table below documents when each variant can arise **for this endpoint specifically**.

| Status | error_category | When (for THIS endpoint) | Example body |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400 | `request_body_was_malformed` | The `scopes=` filter references an unrecognized scope (via `reject_unrecognized_requested_scope`). Also the (effectively unreachable) empty-correlation-identifier check in `validate()`. | `{"error_category":"request_body_was_malformed","error_explanation":"Unrecognized OAuth scope requested: 'admin'"}` |
| 401 | `authentication_credentials_were_missing` | The `x-account-email` header is absent (rejected in the pipeline extractor). | `{"error_category":"authentication_credentials_were_missing","error_explanation":"the 'x-account-email' header was absent"}` |
| 401 | `authentication_credentials_were_invalid` | `x-account-email` is not valid text, does not parse as an email in the extractor, or (defensively) fails `Email::parse` again inside the handler. | `{"error_category":"authentication_credentials_were_invalid","error_explanation":"the account header did not parse into a valid email address"}` |
| 403 | `authorization_was_denied` | No authenticated principal present at the authorization stage (structurally unreachable once `x-account-email` parses). | `{"error_category":"authorization_was_denied","error_explanation":"no authenticated principal was present at the authorization stage"}` |
| 404 | `requested_resource_was_not_found` | Not produced by this handler; listed for completeness of the shared error taxonomy. | `{"error_category":"requested_resource_was_not_found","error_explanation":"..."}` |
| 500 | `upstream_application_failure` | Not produced by this handler (no persistence/upstream call); listed for completeness. | `{"error_category":"upstream_application_failure","error_explanation":"..."}` |

Full `SerializedErrorBody` example:

```json
{
  "error_category": "request_body_was_malformed",
  "error_explanation": "Unrecognized OAuth scope requested: 'admin'"
}
```

#### Internal Processing Pipeline

The handler calls the following real helper functions, in roughly this order:

1. `extract_requesting_principal_for_scope_report(&authorized_request)` — pulls the authorized principal out as an owned `String` via `authorized_principal().as_str()`.
2. `parse_requesting_principal_as_email(principal)` — re-parses that string through `Email::parse`, mapping failure to `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`.
3. `default_granted_oauth_scope_identifiers()` — returns the always-on base set `["openid", "email", "profile"]`.
4. `optional_offline_access_scope_identifiers()` — returns `["offline_access"]`, appended to the base set.
5. `extract_scope_filter_from_correlation(correlation_identifier())` — scans `;`-separated segments of `x-request-id` for a `scopes=` prefix and returns the raw fragment.
6. `parse_optional_requested_scope_filter(raw)` — coerces the raw fragment to `NonEmptyText`; blank/absent → `None`; domain-invalid → mapped-then-dropped to `None`.
7. `split_requested_scope_filter_into_tokens(&filter)` — splits on spaces and commas, trims, drops empties.
8. `reject_unrecognized_requested_scope(requested)` — (per token) errors `RequestBodyWasMalformed` if a token is not recognized.
9. `is_scope_identifier_recognized(scope)` — membership test against base ∪ offline sets (used by #8).
10. `intersect_requested_scopes_with_granted(&granted, &requested)` — intersection preserving granted-set order, de-duplicating requested entries.
11. `serialize_oauth_scope_descriptor_collection(&effective)` → `serialize_single_oauth_scope_descriptor(id)` — builds `{identifier, label, grants_offline_access}` per scope.
12. `describe_oauth_scope_human_label(id)` — maps identifier → human label (used by #11).
13. `determine_scope_report_includes_offline_access(&effective)` — sets the top-level `includes_offline_access` flag.
14. `build_oauth_scopes_report_body(serialized, includes_offline_access)` — assembles the final `{oauth_scopes, scope_count, includes_offline_access}` object.
15. `map_scope_filter_domain_error_to_http_error(domain_failure)` — used only inside #6 for logging parity before the malformed filter is dropped.

#### Edge Cases & Gotchas

- **The scope filter rides in `x-request-id`, not a query or body.** Because the endpoint binds no `Query`/`Json` extractor, the only caller-influenced signal is the correlation identifier. A `scopes=` fragment there is treated as a filter — a surprising, deliberately "debug" coupling. Callers who put arbitrary text after a `;` in their request-id may accidentally trigger filtering.
- **An unrecognized filtered scope hard-fails, but a malformed filter is silently ignored.** Requesting `scopes=admin` returns `400 RequestBodyWasMalformed`, yet a filter that fails `NonEmptyText::parse` is downgraded to "no filter" (returning the full set) rather than erroring — two different failure modes for two different kinds of bad input.
- **Filtering never reorders output.** The result is always emitted in granted-set order (`openid`, `email`, `profile`, `offline_access`) regardless of the order tokens appear in the filter, and duplicate requested tokens collapse to one.
- **The principal is validated twice.** The pipeline extractor already parses `x-account-email` into an `Email`; the handler re-parses it via `Email::parse`. This defensive second parse can (in theory) emit `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid` even though the extractor already vetted the value.
- **`scope_count` reflects the *effective* (post-filter) set, not the full grant.** A filter of `scopes=openid` yields `scope_count: 1`, which can mislead readers into thinking only one scope is granted overall.
- **Missing `x-request-id` defaults to `"unassigned-correlation-identifier"`**, which contains no `scopes=` fragment, so the absence of the header simply means "no filter" — never an error.
- **`State` is intentionally ignored.** The `_application_state` binding means no database, transaction, or upstream call occurs; this endpoint cannot produce `404` or `500` through its own logic.

#### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: How do I filter which scopes are returned?**
A: Append a `scopes=` fragment to your `x-request-id` header, e.g. `x-request-id: corr-1;scopes=openid email`. Yes, in the correlation header. No, there is no query parameter. This is a debug endpoint; it wears its plumbing on the outside.

**Q: I sent `scopes=admin` and got a 400. Is the server broken?**
A: No. `admin` is not a scope this service grants (`openid`, `email`, `profile`, `offline_access` are). Filtering to an unrecognized scope is rejected as `request_body_was_malformed`. Filtering to a recognized-but-not-granted-in-this-context scope simply intersects to nothing.

**Q: Does calling this endpoint change my account's scopes or issue any token?**
A: No. It is a safe, idempotent `GET` that reads static configuration and touches no persistence. It reports what *would* be granted; it grants nothing and issues nothing.

### `GET /api/auth/session` — Retrieve the Authenticated Session Descriptor

#### Synopsis

This endpoint returns the session descriptor for the principal that the request pipeline has already authenticated and authorized. It re-confirms that the principal remains provisioned in the `allowed_emails` allow-list collection, derives a human-facing display name from the local part of the email address, and computes a lightweight session lifecycle descriptor (a status label and an absolute expiry expressed in epoch seconds). No request body is read and no server-side session state is mutated; the response is derived entirely from the authorized principal and the current wall-clock time.

#### Theory & Rationale

In the vocabulary of REST, this is the archetypal *safe, idempotent read*. `GET /api/auth/session` is a projection of the currently authorized principal onto a session-shaped representation, and — this bears repeating, because the reader has demanded that everything bear repeating — it is safe and it is idempotent. It is safe because it induces no observable state change on the server: nothing is created, nothing is rotated, nothing is invalidated, no token is minted. It is idempotent because invoking it once, twice, or ten thousand times in immediate succession yields the same class of representation (the only field that drifts is `expires_at_epoch_seconds`, which tracks the monotone advance of wall-clock time — a property of the universe, not a side effect of the handler). Consequently it is a legitimate target for HTTP caching intermediaries, conditional requests, and speculative prefetch, and it must *never* be repurposed to carry a mutation placed behind a query parameter.

From a Domain-Driven Design standpoint, the handler sits squarely in the HTTP adapter layer (the `alma-http` crate) and is deliberately anemic with respect to domain logic: it parses the transport-level principal string into the `Email` value object (the domain's single source of truth for what constitutes a well-formed address), and it delegates the one genuinely stateful question — "is this principal still provisioned?" — to the `DocumentCollectionPort`, an application-layer port whose concrete adapter the handler neither knows nor cares about. The session lifecycle descriptor is assembled from pure, individually-testable helper functions, keeping the transactional boundary thin and the domain uncontaminated by presentation concerns such as display-name humanization.

#### Authentication & Required Headers

| Header | Required | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x-request-id` | Yes | `x-request-id: 5f3c1b9a-7e2d-4c8a-9f10-2b6d4e1a0c33` | Correlation identifier consumed by the pipeline `originate`/`validate` stages. If empty or whitespace-only, validation fails with `400 request_body_was_malformed` ("the correlation identifier was empty") *before* this handler is ever entered. |
| `x-account-email` | Yes | `x-account-email: ada.lovelace@example.com` | Carries the caller's declared principal. The pipeline establishes this as the authenticated `Email`; this handler reads it via `authorized_principal()`. Absent/blank or malformed principals surface as `401`. |

**The type-state pipeline (`Validated -> Authenticated -> Authorized`).** Access to this handler is gated by Rust's type system, not merely by runtime checks. The request travels through a phantom-typed state machine, `HttpRequestInPipeline<PipelineStage>`, and each transition is a fallible method that consumes the prior state and produces the next:

1. **`RequestHasNotYetBeenValidated`** — the raw origin state, created by `originate(correlation_identifier)`. It carries the correlation id and a not-yet-known principal.
2. **`validate() -> RequestHasBeenValidated`** — rejects an empty/whitespace correlation identifier with `RequestBodyWasMalformed`. Only a validated request can advance.
3. **`authenticate(email) -> RequestHasBeenAuthenticated`** — attaches the authenticated `Email` principal to the request.
4. **`authorize() -> RequestHasBeenAuthorized`** — verifies a principal is actually present; if `declared_principal` is `None`, it returns `AuthorizationWasDenied`.

Because this handler's signature demands `HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>`, it is *statically impossible* to invoke it with a request that has not traversed all three transitions in order — the code simply would not compile otherwise. The handler therefore begins its work already holding a guarantee, encoded in the type, that a principal exists; the runtime re-checks inside the handler (empty-principal rejection, email re-parse) are defensive belt-and-braces confirmations, not the primary gate.

#### Path & Query Parameters

None. This endpoint reads no path segments and no query-string parameters. Any query string supplied by the client is ignored by the handler.

#### Request Body

This endpoint reads **no request body**. Its handler signature accepts only `State(application_state)` and the authorized pipeline request; it does not accept an `axum::Json<T>` extractor, so any body sent by the client is neither deserialized nor inspected. Clients should send no body (and may omit `Content-Type` entirely).

(a) Field table — there are no request-body fields:

| Field | Type | Required | Constraints | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| — | — | — | — | — | No request-body fields are read by this handler. |

```json
  "title": "RetrieveAuthenticatedSessionRequest",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {},
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "description": "This endpoint accepts no request body; the empty object documents that fact."
}
```

```javascript
    "x-request-id": "5f3c1b9a-7e2d-4c8a-9f10-2b6d4e1a0c33",
```

#### Successful Response

Status: `200 OK`. The body is a JSON object with two nested fragments, `profile` and `session`, assembled by `serialize_authenticated_session_response`.

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `profile.authenticated_principal` | string (email) | The authorized principal's canonicalized email address (as returned by `Email::as_str()`). |
| `profile.email_address` | string (email) | The same canonicalized email address; provided as an explicit alias of `authenticated_principal`. |
| `profile.display_name` | string | Human-facing name derived from the local part: separators (`.`, `_`, `-`, `+`) become spaces and each word is capitalized; falls back to the full address if the humanized result is empty. |
| `session.session_status` | string enum | One of `"active"`, `"expiring_soon"` (<= 300 s remaining), or `"expired"` (expiry <= now). |
| `session.expires_at_epoch_seconds` | integer (u64) | Absolute session expiry as whole seconds since the Unix epoch; `now + 3600`, using saturating addition (clamps to `u64::MAX`). |

#### Error Responses

Every error is serialized by `HttpError::into_response` into a `SerializedErrorBody` with exactly two fields, `error_category` and `error_explanation`. The variants below are all `HttpError` variants; the "When" column describes whether and how each can arise for *this specific endpoint*.

| Status | error_category | When (for this endpoint) | Example body |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400 | `request_body_was_malformed` | Not produced by this handler directly. It arises earlier, in the pipeline: `validate()` returns it when the correlation identifier (`x-request-id`) is empty. Also produced by the `From<ApplicationError>` mapping for `DomainInvariantViolated`. | `{"error_category":"request_body_was_malformed","error_explanation":"the correlation identifier was empty"}` |
| 401 | `authentication_credentials_were_missing` | `reject_missing_authenticated_principal` fires when the authorized principal string is empty/whitespace-only. | `{"error_category":"authentication_credentials_were_missing","error_explanation":"no authenticated principal was present on the authorized request"}` |
| 401 | `authentication_credentials_were_invalid` | `parse_authenticated_principal_as_email` fails: the principal string is not a valid `Email` per the domain parser. | `{"error_category":"authentication_credentials_were_invalid","error_explanation":"the authenticated principal was not a valid email address: ..."}` |
| 403 | `authorization_was_denied` | `reject_when_principal_is_not_provisioned` fires: the principal is well-formed and authenticated but is no longer present in the `allowed_emails` allow-list (neither a direct-id match nor an owning-account match). Also emitted by the pipeline `authorize()` stage if a principal is somehow absent. | `{"error_category":"authorization_was_denied","error_explanation":"the authenticated principal 'stranger@example.com' is not provisioned for access"}` |
| 404 | `requested_resource_was_not_found` | Not produced by this handler. Listed for completeness; it is reachable elsewhere via `From<ApplicationError>` for missing-project/missing-resource errors, but this endpoint never returns 404. | `{"error_category":"requested_resource_was_not_found","error_explanation":"..."}` |
| 500 | `upstream_application_failure` | `map_document_collection_failure_to_http_error` wraps any `ApplicationError` returned by the `DocumentCollectionPort` during the provisioning check (`fetch_document` or `list_documents_owned_by`). | `{"error_category":"upstream_application_failure","error_explanation":"the session provisioning check failed: ..."}` |

Full example of a serialized error body:

```json
{
  "error_category": "authorization_was_denied",
  "error_explanation": "the authenticated principal 'stranger@example.com' is not provisioned for access"
}
```

#### Internal Processing Pipeline

The handler orchestrates the following real helper functions, in order:

1. `extract_authenticated_principal_identifier(&authorized_request)` — reads the authorized principal from the pipeline request via `authorized_principal().as_str()` and returns it as an owned `String`.
2. `reject_missing_authenticated_principal(&raw)` — returns `AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing` if the principal string is empty or whitespace-only.
3. `parse_authenticated_principal_as_email(raw)` — parses the string into a domain `Email`, mapping parse failures to `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`.
4. `confirm_authenticated_principal_is_provisioned(&document_collection, &email)` — checks the `allowed_emails` collection: first a direct `fetch_document` by email id, then a fallback `list_documents_owned_by`; returns `bool`.
5. `allowed_emails_collection_name()` — returns the `ALLOWED_EMAILS_COLLECTION_NAME` constant (`"allowed_emails"`), used inside the provisioning check.
6. `reject_when_principal_is_not_provisioned(is_provisioned, &email)` — returns `AuthorizationWasDenied` when the provisioning check came back `false`.
7. `derive_display_name_from_email_local_part(&email)` — humanizes the local part into a display name (separator-splitting, capitalization, fallback to full address).
8. `capitalize_first_character(word)` — uppercases the first character of a word, leaving the remainder unchanged (used by the display-name derivation).
9. `current_epoch_seconds()` — reads wall-clock time as whole seconds since the Unix epoch, treating pre-epoch clocks as `0`.
10. `default_session_time_to_live_seconds()` — returns the fixed TTL of `3_600` seconds (one hour).
11. `compute_session_expiry_epoch_seconds(now, ttl)` — `now.saturating_add(ttl)` to derive the absolute expiry.
12. `determine_session_status_label(now, expiry)` — returns `"expired"`, `"expiring_soon"` (<= 300 s left), or `"active"`.
13. `build_authenticated_user_profile_fragment(&email, &display_name)` — builds the `profile` JSON fragment.
14. `build_session_lifecycle_fragment(status_label, expiry)` — builds the `session` JSON fragment.
15. `serialize_authenticated_session_response(profile, lifecycle)` — merges the two fragments into the final response body.
16. `map_document_collection_failure_to_http_error(port_failure)` — wraps `ApplicationError` from the port into `UpstreamApplicationFailure`.

#### Edge Cases & Gotchas

- **The TTL is hard-coded and not remembered.** `default_session_time_to_live_seconds()` always returns `3_600`. There is no server-side session store; `expires_at_epoch_seconds` is recomputed as `now + 3600` on every single call. Two rapid calls will report two different expiries, and neither reflects any persisted session — the "session" is a computed fiction rebuilt per request.
- **`session_status` can never actually be `"expired"` in a fresh response.** Because expiry is `now + 3600` computed within the same request, the remaining time is ~3600 s, so a live call always yields `"active"`. The `"expired"` and `"expiring_soon"` branches are reachable only in unit tests (or via clock pathologies), not in normal operation.
- **Provisioning is re-checked on every read.** Even though the pipeline already authorized the principal, `confirm_authenticated_principal_is_provisioned` hits the document collection twice in the worst case (a `fetch_document`, then a `list_documents_owned_by` fallback). A principal deprovisioned mid-session gets `403` on the very next `GET /api/auth/session`.
- **Display-name humanization is lossy and opinionated.** The local part is split on `.`, `_`, `-`, and `+`, each token capitalized, and joined with spaces. `grace_hopper-navy+tag@...` becomes `"Grace Hopper Navy Tag"`. A local part that is entirely separators (or otherwise humanizes to empty) falls back to the full address — the client always gets a non-empty `display_name`.
- **`authenticated_principal` and `email_address` are always identical.** Both are `Email::as_str()`. They are intentionally duplicated for client convenience; do not assume they can ever diverge.
- **Email canonicalization happens on parse.** `Email::parse` canonicalizes (e.g. lowercasing, per the domain parser); the address echoed back may differ in case from what the client sent in `x-account-email`. The provisioning lookup uses the canonicalized form as the collection key.
- **Clock-before-epoch is swallowed, not surfaced.** `current_epoch_seconds()` returns `0` rather than erroring if the system clock is before the Unix epoch, so expiry math degrades gracefully instead of panicking.

#### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Can I send a request body or query parameters to influence the session?**
A: No. The handler reads neither. There is no `Json<T>` extractor and no query extractor. Anything you send is silently ignored.

**Q: Does calling this endpoint extend, refresh, or renew my session?**
A: No. It is a safe, idempotent read. The reported expiry is recomputed as `now + 3600` each call, but nothing is persisted, so there is no session to extend. If you want token rotation, use `POST /api/auth/refresh-token`.

**Q: I got a `403 authorization_was_denied` even though I was authenticated a second ago. Why?**
A: Authentication and authorization by the pipeline are necessary but not sufficient. This handler additionally re-confirms that your email is still provisioned in the `allowed_emails` allow-list. If your address was removed from the allow-list, you are authenticated (we know who you are) but no longer authorized to hold a session, hence `403`.

### `POST /api/auth/refresh-token` — Rotate the Caller's Refresh Token

#### Synopsis

This endpoint accepts a refresh token that the authenticated principal currently holds, verifies that the presented token exactly matches the token on record for that principal, and — if and only if it matches — mints a brand-new refresh token, atomically replaces the old record with the new one, and returns the freshly rotated token to the caller. It is the single supported mechanism by which a client trades a still-valid refresh token for its successor, implementing a strict one-in-one-out rotation discipline. The endpoint reads exactly one field from the request body (`presented_refresh_token`, with a legacy alias of `refresh_token`), performs a constant-time-style secret comparison against persisted state, and never returns the old token under any circumstance.

#### Theory & Rationale

From a REST-semantics standpoint this operation is deliberately modeled as a `POST` rather than a `PUT` or `GET`, and that choice is neither accidental nor negotiable. Refresh-token rotation is emphatically **not safe** (it mutates server-side state on every successful invocation) and it is emphatically **not idempotent** (each successful call destroys the previously valid token and manufactures a distinct new one, so replaying the same request with the same body twice will succeed the first time and fail the second, because the token presented on the replay no longer matches the newly stored value). A `PUT` would falsely advertise idempotency to intermediaries, caches, and retry-happy client libraries; a `GET` would falsely advertise safety and cacheability of what is in fact a security-critical, side-effecting credential exchange. `POST` is the only verb whose contract honestly describes "submit this credential, and in exchange I will perform a non-repeatable state transition and hand you a new one."

Within the Domain-Driven Design layering of `alma-http`, this handler sits squarely in the HTTP category layer (`crates/http/src/categories/auth/`) and is intentionally thin-but-verbose: it orchestrates a sequence of small, individually-testable helper functions, delegating all persistence to the `DocumentCollectionPort` application port rather than reaching into any concrete store. The principal identity is not trusted from the body — it is lifted from the type-state pipeline's `authorized_principal()` — which places the authorization boundary firmly upstream of business logic and keeps the aggregate ("this principal's single active refresh token") as the unit of consistency. Note a small but real leak of infrastructure knowledge into this handler: because `collections.rs` declares only `ALLOWED_EMAILS_COLLECTION_NAME`, the refresh-token collection name (`auth_refresh_tokens`) is owned as a local constant here rather than in the shared collections module.

#### Authentication & Required Headers

This endpoint is fully protected. The request must traverse the entire type-state pipeline and arrive as an `HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>` before this handler's body executes at all. The principal (an email address) is extracted from the pipeline, not from the body or from any header the client controls directly for identity purposes.

| Header | Required | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x-request-id` | Recommended | `x-request-id: 5f2c9b1e-7a3d-4c2a-9f11-2b8e0d6a44c1` | Correlation identifier echoed through logs and traces. Not read by this handler's own code, but honored by the surrounding pipeline/middleware for observability. If omitted, one is typically synthesized upstream. |
| `x-account-email` | Yes (identity) | `x-account-email: scholar@example.org` | Carries the caller's account email into the authentication stage. This value becomes the `authorized_principal()` that this handler reads; it is re-parsed into a validated `Email` before use. It must be a syntactically valid email address. |

**The type-state pipeline (`Validated` → `Authenticated` → `Authorized`).** Requests to this route are not handed raw to the handler. They are progressively refined through a compile-time-enforced type-state machine, where each stage is a distinct Rust type and it is impossible to reach the next stage without having provably satisfied the previous one:

1. **Validated** — the incoming request's shape, method, and basic invariants have been checked. The request now carries a marker proving structural validity.
2. **Authenticated** — the caller's identity (their email principal) has been established from the credential-bearing headers (e.g. `x-account-email`). Failure here surfaces as `401 AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing` / `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`.
3. **Authorized** — the authenticated principal has been confirmed to be permitted to perform this operation. Only an `HttpRequestInPipeline<RequestHasBeenAuthorized>` can be passed as the `authorized_request` extractor argument to this handler. Because the handler's signature demands the `RequestHasBeenAuthorized` type parameter, the compiler itself guarantees that no unauthenticated or unauthorized request can ever reach the handler body — the failure would be a type error, not a runtime check.

The practical consequence: by the time `rotate_refresh_token_handler` runs, `authorized_request.authorized_principal()` is guaranteed to yield a valid, authenticated, authorized identity. The handler nonetheless re-parses it into an `Email` and treats a parse failure as an *internal inconsistency* (`AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid`), not a client error.

#### Path & Query Parameters

None. This endpoint takes no path segments beyond the fixed literal `/api/auth/refresh-token` and reads no query-string parameters whatsoever.

| Name | In | Type | Required | Constraints | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| — | — | — | — | — | — | None. |

#### Request Body

The handler deserializes the body as an untyped `serde_json::Value` and then reads exactly one logical field out of it. The primary field name is `presented_refresh_token`; if that key is absent, the handler falls back to reading `refresh_token` (a legacy alias). No other body fields are read, inspected, or validated — any additional keys are silently ignored.

**(a) Fields the handler reads**

| Field | Type | Required | Constraints | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `presented_refresh_token` | string | Yes (or provide `refresh_token`) | Must be a JSON string; non-empty after parse; after trimming, length ≥ 8 characters; characters restricted to ASCII alphanumerics plus `-` and `_`. | none | The refresh token the caller currently holds and wishes to rotate. Must exactly match the token stored for the authenticated principal. |
| `refresh_token` | string | Only if `presented_refresh_token` is absent | Same constraints as `presented_refresh_token`. | none | Legacy alias for `presented_refresh_token`. Used only as a fallback when the primary key is missing. |

**(b) JSON Schema (draft 2020-12)**

```json
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",

  "title": "RotateRefreshTokenRequest",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "presented_refresh_token": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 8,
      "pattern": "^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$",
      "description": "The refresh token the caller currently holds and wishes to rotate."
    },
    "refresh_token": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 8,
      "pattern": "^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$",

    }
  },

    { "required": ["presented_refresh_token"] },

  ],

}
```

#### Successful Response

On success the handler returns `200 OK` with a JSON object containing the newly minted token, its lifetime in seconds, and a fixed token type discriminator. The response body is built by `build_rotated_token_response_body`.

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `rotated_token` | string | The freshly generated refresh token (a UUIDv4 string, 36 characters). This replaces the caller's previous token. |
| `expires_in_seconds` | number (integer) | Lifetime granted to the rotated token, in seconds. Currently the constant `ROTATED_TOKEN_LIFETIME_SECONDS` = `3600`. |
| `token_type` | string | Always the literal `"refresh"`. |

```json
}
```
