#### Error Responses

Errors are serialized by `HttpError` into a `SerializedErrorBody` of the shape `{ "error_category", "error_explanation" }`. The table below lists every `HttpError` variant and how (or whether) it can arise for *this specific endpoint*.

| Status | error_category | When (for THIS endpoint) | Example body |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400 | `RequestBodyWasMalformed` | The correlation identifier failed validation (blank after trimming) — rare here because the extractor supplies a non-empty default. Also mapped from `ApplicationError::DomainInvariantViolated` bubbling up from the collection port. | `{"error_category":"RequestBodyWasMalformed","error_explanation":"the correlation identifier was empty"}` |
| 401 | `AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing` | The `x-account-email` header is absent. | `{"error_category":"AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing","error_explanation":"the 'x-account-email' header was absent"}` |
| 401 | `AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid` | The `x-account-email` header is not valid text, or does not parse into a valid email address. | `{"error_category":"AuthenticationCredentialsWereInvalid","error_explanation":"the account header did not parse into a valid email address"}` |
| 403 | `AuthorizationWasDenied` | No authenticated principal was present at the authorization stage (defensive; unreachable in normal flow). Also mapped from `ApplicationError::AuthorizationWasDenied` returned by the collection port. | `{"error_category":"AuthorizationWasDenied","error_explanation":"no authenticated principal was present at the authorization stage"}` |
| 404 | `RequestedResourceWasNotFound` | The collection port returns `ApplicationError::RequestedProjectCouldNotBeLocated` or `RequestedResourceCouldNotBeLocated` (e.g. the backing collection itself is missing). | `{"error_category":"RequestedResourceWasNotFound","error_explanation":"the requested resource could not be located"}` |
| 500 | `UpstreamApplicationFailure` | Any other `ApplicationError` from `list_documents` (connection failure, serialization error, unexpected persistence fault). | `{"error_category":"UpstreamApplicationFailure","error_explanation":"the underlying document store was unavailable"}` |

Full example error body:

```json
{
  "error_category": "AuthenticationCredentialsWereMissing",
  "error_explanation": "the 'x-account-email' header was absent"
}
```

#### Internal Processing Pipeline

The handler body invokes the following real helper functions, in order:

1. `resolve_requesting_account_from_principal(authorized_request.authorized_principal())` — converts the authorized `Email` principal into a `String`; the result is intentionally discarded into `_requesting_account` to anchor the request to a concrete account for audit honesty.
2. `extract_optional_study_type_name_filter(&authorized_request)` — reads the correlation identifier, splits on `name:`, trims the tail, and returns `Some(filter)` or `None` (empty tail ⇒ `None` ⇒ return everything).
3. `fetch_all_study_type_template_documents(application_state.document_collection.as_ref())` — calls `DocumentCollectionPort::list_documents(STUDY_TYPE_TEMPLATES_COLLECTION_NAME)` and maps any error via `map_application_error_to_http_error`.
4. `map_application_error_to_http_error(application_error)` — explicit `ApplicationError` → `HttpError` classifier (see Error Responses table).
5. `filter_study_type_templates_by_name_substring(all_stored_documents, &name_filter)` — invoked only when a filter is present; keeps documents whose extracted name contains the (lower-cased) filter substring.
6. `extract_study_type_name_from_body(&document_body)` — used by the filter and the projector; reads `study_type_name` → `name` → `title`, rejecting blanks.
7. `render_study_type_template_documents_into_summaries(documents_to_render)` — maps each document through the projector and then sorts.
8. `project_stored_document_to_study_type_template_summary(&stored_document)` — builds one summary object (identifier, owner, name, section count, headings, description preview).
9. `count_sections_in_study_type_template_body`, `collect_section_headings_from_body`, `extract_section_outline_from_body` — compute section metadata for the projection.
10. `extract_study_type_description_preview_from_body(&document_body, 160)` — whitespace-collapse and truncate the description to a 160-char preview.
11. `sort_study_type_template_summaries_by_name_ascending(&mut rendered_summaries)` — case-insensitive ascending sort by `study_type_name`.
12. `count_returned_study_type_templates(&rendered_summaries)` — returns the vector length as `total_count`.
13. `build_study_type_template_listing_response(rendered_summaries, total_count)` — wraps the summaries and count into the final `{ study_type_templates, total_count }` JSON, returned inside `Json(..)`.

#### Edge Cases & Gotchas

- **The filter is not a query parameter — it is hidden in `x-request-id`.** To filter by name you must set the correlation-identifier header to something containing `name:<value>`. There is no `?name=` support. This conflates the correlation/tracing channel with a business filter, so a genuine correlation ID that happens to contain the literal `name:` will be interpreted as a filter.
- **`split_once("name:")` splits on the *first* occurrence and keeps the tail.** If your correlation ID is `name:foo name:bar`, the filter becomes `foo name:bar`, not `bar`. Only a single, clean `name:<value>` directive behaves intuitively.
- **An empty or whitespace-only filter tail means "return everything."** `x-request-id: name:` (nothing after) and `x-request-id: name:    ` both yield `None`, so no filtering is applied.
- **`study_type_name` has a three-key fallback and then falls back to the identifier.** The name is read from `study_type_name`, then `name`, then `title`; if none is a non-blank string, the summary's `study_type_name` becomes the raw `template_identifier`. Sorting therefore sometimes orders by identifier, not by any human name.
- **Section headings are silently dropped when unnamed.** A section object lacking `heading`/`title`/`name` (or having only blanks) is counted in `section_count` but contributes nothing to `section_headings`. So `section_count` and `section_headings.length` can legitimately differ.
- **Description preview truncation counts Unicode scalar values, not bytes.** It collapses all runs of whitespace to single spaces, then truncates at 160 `char`s and appends `...`. Multi-byte characters count as one; there is no word-boundary awareness, so it can cut mid-word.
- **The requesting account never affects results.** Authentication/authorization gate access, but the listing is fetched via `list_documents` (collection-wide), never `list_documents_owned_by`. Two different authenticated users see the same catalogue.

#### Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: How do I paginate this endpoint?**
A: You do not. There is no `limit`, `offset`, `cursor`, or `page` anywhere in the handler. It fetches the entire collection, projects all of it, sorts all of it, and returns all of it. If the collection is large, so is your response.

**Q: Why is `total_count` in the response when the array already has a length?**
A: For your convenience, and for the convenience of consumers allergic to `array.length`. It is computed as `rendered_summaries.len()` and will always equal `study_type_templates.length`. It is not a total-before-filtering count — it is the count of what you were actually handed.

**Q: I sent a JSON body describing the filter I want. Why was it ignored?**
A: Because this is a `GET` handler that binds no body extractor. It reads `State` and the authorized-request marker, and nothing else. Put your filter in the `x-request-id` header as `name:<value>`, as documented, and stop sending bodies to GET endpoints.

# Part III — Appendices

## Appendix A: Glossary

> *A terminology reference for the `alma-http` backend, written for the reader who
> has arrived here with no prior context and who deserves a definition rather than
> a wink. Terms are ordered alphabetically. Where a term has a precise meaning
> inside this codebase that differs from its colloquial meaning in the wider
> industry, the codebase meaning wins and is stated as such.*

**Account.** The security principal on whose behalf a request is executed. In
`alma-http` an account is identified by an email address carried on the
`x-account-email` request header and validated into an `Email` value object
before it is permitted to influence anything. There is no session, no cookie, and
no server-side account record beyond the emails that appear in the allowed-emails
collection; the account is, for the duration of a single request, simply the
validated email and nothing more.

**Adapter.** In the ports-and-adapters (hexagonal) architecture, an adapter is a
concrete implementation that connects the application core to the outside world.
The `alma-http` crate is itself the *inbound* adapter (it adapts HTTP into
application commands and queries). The in-memory store, the AI completion
generator, and the literature lookup client are *outbound* adapters (they adapt
the application's outbound ports into concrete, if simulated, behaviour). See
Appendix F for the important caveat that the outbound adapters shipped here are
deterministic stubs.

**Application core.** The provider-agnostic, transport-agnostic centre of the
system. It holds the domain model, the value objects, the use-case handlers, and
the outbound port traits. It does not know that HTTP exists. Every symbol the
HTTP layer imports from the core is imported precisely so that HTTP concerns stay
out of the core.

**Boundary.** Any place where an untyped, untrusted value from the outside world
is turned into a typed, trusted value inside the system — or the reverse. The
entire design philosophy of `alma-http` is that validation happens *at the
boundary*, exactly once, so that everything deeper than the boundary can assume
correctness rather than re-checking it.

**Category (error).** The stable, machine-readable string that classifies an
error response. It appears as the `error_category` field of the serialized error
body. There are exactly six categories; they are enumerated exhaustively in
Appendix E. Categories are contract; explanations are commentary.

**Collection.** A named logical grouping of stored documents inside the store,
analogous to a table in a relational database or a collection in a document
database. Each collection has a stable string name defined once as a `const` in a
`collections.rs` module. The full registry of collection names is Appendix D.

**Command.** A request that intends to change state (create, update, delete). In
the CQRS-influenced vocabulary of the core, commands are separated conceptually
from queries even where the same store backs both.

**Completion.** The text produced by the AI generation port in response to a
prompt. On the wire it is carried by the `GeneratedCompletion` type (Appendix C)
in its `produced_text` field. In this build the completion is generated by a
deterministic stub; it is structurally a real completion and semantically a
simulation. See Appendix F.

**CQRS.** Command Query Responsibility Segregation — the pattern of modelling
state-changing operations (commands) separately from state-reading operations
(queries). The core aspires to it; the HTTP layer merely reflects it in the shape
of its handlers.

**Document.** The unit of persistence. A stored document is represented by the
`StoredDocument` type (Appendix C), carrying a `document_identifier`, an
`owning_account`, and an opaque `document_body`. Documents live inside
collections.

**Domain invariant.** A rule that must always hold for a domain value to be
valid — for example, that an email is well-formed, or that a project name is not
empty. When an invariant is violated during construction of a value object, the
construction fails, and that failure is ultimately surfaced to the caller as a
`request_body_was_malformed` error (Appendix E).

**Email.** A value object wrapping a validated email address. It is the identity
of an account. Construction rejects anything that is not a syntactically
plausible email, which is why nothing downstream ever has to ask "is this a real
email?" — by the time a value has the `Email` type, the question is already
answered.

**Explanation.** The human-readable, free-text description attached to an error
response, carried in the `error_explanation` field of the serialized error body.
Unlike the category, the explanation is *not* a stable contract: its wording may
change between versions and it is intended for a human reading logs, not for a
program to branch on.

**Extractor.** In axum terms, a type that knows how to pull a typed value out of
an inbound request (headers, body, path, query). The `alma-http` request pipeline
leans on extractors to move validation to the boundary.

**Handler.** The function that services one endpoint. It receives already-typed,
already-validated inputs, invokes the appropriate application use case, and maps
the result back to an HTTP response. Handlers are deliberately thin; the thinking
lives in the core.

**Hexagonal architecture.** See *Ports and adapters*. The two names describe the
same idea: a core surrounded by a ring of adapters, with the core depending on
abstract ports rather than concrete transports.

**Identifier.** A stable, opaque string that names a stored document uniquely
within its collection. Carried as `document_identifier` on `StoredDocument`.
Clients should treat identifiers as opaque tokens and never attempt to parse
meaning out of them.

**In-memory store.** The concrete persistence adapter used in this build. It
keeps all documents in process memory. It is real code with real semantics for
the duration of the process, and it forgets everything the moment the process
exits. See Appendix F.

**Owning account.** The email of the account that owns a stored document, carried
as `owning_account` on `StoredDocument`. Ownership is the basis for authorization
decisions: a request that is authenticated as one account may be denied access to
a document owned by another.

**Port.** An abstract interface (in Rust, a trait) that the application core
defines to describe something it needs from the outside world — a way to store
documents, a way to generate completions, a way to look up publications. Ports are
implemented by adapters. The core depends on ports; it never depends on adapters
directly.

**Ports and adapters.** The architectural style, also called hexagonal
architecture, in which the application core defines ports and the surrounding
infrastructure provides adapters. The central benefit is that the core can be
tested and reasoned about without any real transport or database, and that
adapters (including stubs) can be swapped without touching the core.

**Publication.** A bibliographic record returned by the literature lookup port.
On the wire it is a `PublicationSummary` (Appendix C) carrying a
`publication_title`, a `digital_object_identifier`, and an `originating_source`.

**Query.** A request that reads state without changing it. The read half of CQRS.

**Request identifier.** A correlation token carried on the `x-request-id` header,
used to tie together log lines and responses belonging to the same inbound
request. It is an observability aid, not a security mechanism.

**Store.** The persistence abstraction as a whole — the port plus whichever
adapter implements it. In this build the adapter is the in-memory store.

**Stub.** A deterministic stand-in adapter that satisfies a port's contract with
predictable, hard-coded-ish behaviour rather than a real integration. The AI and
literature adapters in this build are stubs. This is a first-class design fact,
not an accident; see Appendix F.

**Type-state.** A technique in which the *type* of a value encodes *where in a
process* that value is, so that operations that are only valid at a certain stage
are only callable on the type that represents that stage. The request pipeline
uses type-state so that, for example, an unauthenticated request simply does not
have a type on which the authenticated-only operations exist.

**Upstream failure.** An error that originates deeper than the HTTP layer — inside
the application core or one of its adapters — and that does not map to any more
specific category. It surfaces as the `upstream_application_failure` category with
HTTP status 500. It is the catch-all, and its presence in a response means the
fault is on the server side.

**Value object.** A small, immutable type whose identity is its value and whose
construction enforces a domain invariant. `Email`, `NonEmptyText`, and
`ProjectName` are the canonical examples. Value objects are the mechanism by which
"validate at the boundary" becomes "cannot possibly be invalid deeper in."

---

## Appendix B: HTTP Status Code Reference

> *Every status code that the `alma-http` surface can emit, what it means in
> general HTTP terms, and what it means specifically here. The surface is
> deliberately narrow: it uses a small, disciplined set of codes and never
> improvises. If you receive a code not listed in this table, treat it as coming
> from infrastructure in front of the application (a proxy, a load balancer, the
> runtime), not from `alma-http` itself.*

| Code | Reason phrase | General meaning | Meaning inside `alma-http` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `200` | OK | The request succeeded and the response carries the result. | The default success code for every handler that returns a body. A `200` is only produced after all validation, authentication, and authorization have passed and the use case completed. |
| `400` | Bad Request | The request was malformed and the server will not process it. | Emitted for the `request_body_was_malformed` category: the JSON body could not be parsed, a required field was absent, or a value violated a domain invariant during value-object construction. The fault is on the client. |
| `401` | Unauthorized | The request lacks valid authentication credentials. | Emitted for both `authentication_credentials_were_missing` (no `x-account-email` header) and `authentication_credentials_were_invalid` (the header was present but did not validate into an `Email`). The client must supply valid credentials and retry. |
| `403` | Forbidden | The server understood the request but refuses to authorize it. | Emitted for the `authorization_was_denied` category: the caller was authenticated but is not permitted to act on the targeted resource — for example, touching a document owned by another account. Retrying with the same credentials will not help. |
| `404` | Not Found | The requested resource does not exist. | Emitted for the `requested_resource_was_not_found` category: no document with the requested identifier exists in the targeted collection (or the project could not be located). Note that ownership checks may also surface as `404` in cases where revealing existence would itself leak information. |
| `429` | Too Many Requests | The client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. | Emitted by the rate-limiting cross-cutting layer, not by an individual handler. It sits in front of the handlers; a `429` means the request never reached its handler. Back off and retry later. |
| `500` | Internal Server Error | The server encountered an unexpected condition. | Emitted for the `upstream_application_failure` category: any error originating in the application core or an adapter that does not map to a more specific category. The fault is on the server. |

**Codes deliberately not used.** The surface does not emit `201 Created`,
`204 No Content`, `202 Accepted`, `3xx` redirects, `405 Method Not Allowed`
(unmatched method/path combinations are handled by the router before a handler is
selected), or `422 Unprocessable Entity` (validation failures are reported as
`400`, on the principle that a body which fails a domain invariant is malformed
for this API's purposes). This narrowness is intentional: a small vocabulary of
codes is easier to consume correctly than a large one.

---

## Appendix C: Canonical Data Types

> *The four types below are the load-bearing shapes of the entire surface. Almost
> every endpoint speaks in terms of one or more of them. Field names on the wire
> are exactly as written; the JSON casing convention (verbose `snake_case`) is
> preserved. Each type is given prose, a field table, and a JSON Schema
> (draft 2020-12).*

### C.1 `StoredDocument`

The universal persistence envelope. Anything the store holds is a
`StoredDocument`: a stable identifier, the account that owns it, and an opaque
body whose internal shape depends on the collection it lives in. The HTTP layer
does not interpret `document_body`; it is passed through as an opaque JSON value.

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `document_identifier` | string | Stable, opaque, unique-within-collection identifier. Treat as a token; do not parse. |
| `owning_account` | string (email) | Email of the account that owns this document. Basis for authorization. |
| `document_body` | object | Opaque, collection-specific payload. The HTTP layer does not interpret its contents. |

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "https://alma.example/schemas/StoredDocument.json",
  "title": "StoredDocument",
  "type": "object",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "required": ["document_identifier", "owning_account", "document_body"],
  "properties": {
    "document_identifier": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1,
      "description": "Stable, opaque, unique-within-collection identifier."
    },
    "owning_account": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "email",
      "description": "Email of the account that owns this document."
    },
    "document_body": {
      "type": "object",
      "description": "Opaque, collection-specific payload; not interpreted by the HTTP layer."
    }
  }
}
```

### C.2 `GeneratedCompletion`

The output of the AI generation port. A single field carrying the produced text.
In this build the text is produced by a deterministic stub (Appendix F); the shape
is nonetheless the real, permanent contract.

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `produced_text` | string | The text produced by the generation port in response to the prompt. |

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "https://alma.example/schemas/GeneratedCompletion.json",
  "title": "GeneratedCompletion",
  "type": "object",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "required": ["produced_text"],
  "properties": {
    "produced_text": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "The text produced by the generation port in response to the prompt."
    }
  }
}
```

### C.3 `PublicationSummary`

A single bibliographic record returned by the literature lookup port. The
`digital_object_identifier` is the canonical DOI; the `originating_source` names
which bibliographic source the record came from.

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `publication_title` | string | The title of the publication. |
| `digital_object_identifier` | string | The DOI of the publication. |
| `originating_source` | string | The bibliographic source from which this record originated. |

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "https://alma.example/schemas/PublicationSummary.json",
  "title": "PublicationSummary",
  "type": "object",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "required": ["publication_title", "digital_object_identifier", "originating_source"],
  "properties": {
    "publication_title": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1,
      "description": "The title of the publication."
    },
    "digital_object_identifier": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "The DOI of the publication."
    },
    "originating_source": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "The bibliographic source from which this record originated."
    }
  }
}
```

### C.4 `SerializedErrorBody`

The wire shape of every error response, without exception. Two fields: a stable
machine-readable `error_category` (see Appendix E for the closed set of values)
and a free-text, non-contractual `error_explanation`.

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `error_category` | string (enum) | Stable, machine-readable category. One of the six values in Appendix E. |
| `error_explanation` | string | Human-readable description. Not a stable contract; do not branch on it. |

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "https://alma.example/schemas/SerializedErrorBody.json",
  "title": "SerializedErrorBody",
  "type": "object",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "required": ["error_category", "error_explanation"],
  "properties": {
    "error_category": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Stable, machine-readable error category.",
      "enum": [
        "request_body_was_malformed",
        "authentication_credentials_were_missing",
        "authentication_credentials_were_invalid",
        "authorization_was_denied",
        "requested_resource_was_not_found",
        "upstream_application_failure"
      ]
    },
    "error_explanation": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Human-readable description; not a stable contract."
    }
  }
}
```

## Appendix E: Error Category Reference

> *The complete, closed set of `error_category` values. There are exactly six.
> The set is closed: a well-behaved client can enumerate every category it will
> ever see and handle each explicitly. Each row gives the category string, the
> HTTP status it always maps to, the fault side (client or server), and guidance
> on how a client should respond.*

| Category | Status | Fault | What it means | Recommended client response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `request_body_was_malformed` | `400` | Client | The body could not be parsed, a required field was missing, or a value violated a domain invariant during value-object construction. Also the destination for a violated `DomainInvariantViolated` from the core. | Fix the request payload. Do not blindly retry the same body. |
| `authentication_credentials_were_missing` | `401` | Client | No authentication credential (the `x-account-email` header) was supplied. | Attach a valid `x-account-email` header and retry. |
| `authentication_credentials_were_invalid` | `401` | Client | A credential was supplied but failed to validate into an `Email`. | Correct the credential and retry. |
| `authorization_was_denied` | `403` | Client | The caller was authenticated but is not permitted to act on the targeted resource (e.g. a document owned by another account). | Do not retry with the same credentials; obtain access or target a resource you own. |
| `requested_resource_was_not_found` | `404` | Client | No document with the requested identifier exists in the targeted collection, or the project could not be located. Sourced from `RequestedProjectCouldNotBeLocated` and `RequestedResourceCouldNotBeLocated` in the core. | Verify the identifier. The resource may never have existed or may have been removed. |
| `upstream_application_failure` | `500` | Server | Catch-all for any application-core or adapter error that does not map to a more specific category. | Retry with backoff; if it persists, it is a server-side problem to be reported. |

**On the category/explanation split.** The `error_category` is the contract:
its value set is closed, stable across versions, and safe to branch on
programmatically. The `error_explanation` is commentary: free text intended for a
human reading a log, subject to rewording between versions, and never to be parsed
by a program. Build client logic on the category; show the explanation to people.

**On the mapping being total.** Every error that reaches the HTTP boundary is
translated into exactly one of these six categories. The core's richer error enum
is collapsed at the `From<ApplicationError> for HttpError` boundary: located/not-
located failures become `requested_resource_was_not_found`, authorization denials
become `authorization_was_denied`, domain-invariant violations become
`request_body_was_malformed`, and everything else — the open-ended tail — becomes
`upstream_application_failure`. There is no seventh outcome.

---

## Appendix F: A Note on Stubs

> *Read this appendix before you draw any conclusion about what this build
> actually integrates with. It is the single most important caveat in the entire
> reference.*

The `alma-http` surface documented here is **structurally real and end-to-end
simulated.** Every shape, every status code, every error category, every field
name, and every collection key is exactly what the code produces. What is
*simulated* is the behaviour behind three of the outbound adapters.

**The AI generation adapter is a deterministic stub.** When an endpoint returns a
`GeneratedCompletion`, the `produced_text` was not generated by any large language
model. It was produced by a deterministic stand-in that satisfies the generation
port's contract with predictable output. The *shape* of the response — and the
fact that it flows through the same validation, authentication, and error-mapping
pipeline as everything else — is genuine. The *content* is manufactured.

**The literature lookup adapter is a deterministic stub.** When an endpoint
returns `PublicationSummary` records, those records were not fetched from any real
bibliographic database or DOI resolver. The `digital_object_identifier` and
`originating_source` fields are populated by the stub. Again: the shape is real,
the plumbing is real, the data is simulated.

**The store is in-memory.** Persistence is provided by an in-memory store adapter.
It behaves like a store for the lifetime of the process — you can create a
`StoredDocument`, read it back, and observe ownership-based authorization exactly
as a real database would enforce it — and it forgets everything the instant the
process exits. There is no disk, no external database, no durability across
restarts.

**Why this is a feature, not a shortcoming.** The whole point of ports-and-
adapters is that the application core cannot tell the difference between a stub
adapter and a production one. Because the stubs honour the same port contracts,
every response you observe is *contractually identical* to what a fully integrated
deployment would produce — same types, same casing, same status codes, same error
taxonomy. You can build and test a client against this surface with complete
confidence in its shape, and swap the stubs for real adapters later without the
client noticing. What you must **not** do is treat the simulated *content* —
generated text, DOIs, sources, or any persisted data surviving a restart — as
authoritative. It is structurally real and semantically simulated. Plan
accordingly.
